title: AI watermarks
text:
AI Text Watermark
An AI text watermark is not a hidden character, a secret tag, or special file metadata. Instead, text watermarks are mathematical patterns in word choice
A brief explanation how LLM works

Whenever an AI generates a sentence, it often has multiple words to pick next (e.g., choosing between quick, fast, or rapid).
AI will choose a word based on words probability (Top-p/Top-K sampling)

A brief idea of AI watermark

If I set rapid in the Watermark list, then AI-generated text will be in favor of choosing rapid over other synonyms
If we have a bag of the Watermark list, as long as a “statistically significant” amount of the word occurs in the Watermark list then I will believe it is an AI-generated content

title: AI watermarks
text:
Challenges of developing watermarks

Imperceptibility :

Language conventions
Content accuracy, highly technical writing
Mathematical formula writing

Robustness :

Robust to reformatting, paraphrasing

Detectability & Security :

Low false positive rate, cannot reverse attack the algorithm

title: AI watermarks
text:
Generating watermarks

Before generating word: The AI looks at the word it just typed and uses a secret rule to secretly split the entire dictionary into 50% Green words and 50% Red words.
During generating words: The AI gives Green words a subtle extra boost (\(\delta\)), making them far more likely to be chosen while keeping the sentence completely natural.

title: AI watermarks
text: Illustration of the algorithm

title: AI watermarks
text:
Deciphering watermarks

Detecting a text: A human naturally lands on Green about 50% of the time (like flipping a fair coin), but the watermarked AI lands on Green 75%–85% of the time.
The final judgement: If a 200-word paragraph hits Green far too often to be pure luck, a quick probability test proves it came from the AI.

title: AI watermarks
section: Shortest detectable length for a watermark
text:
Shortest detectable length for a watermark

Assuming a 50% (\(\gamma\)) Green/Red split
The Expectation of Z-test statistics given a sample of T tokens is: \[
\mathbb{E}[z] = \frac{(\bar{p}_G - \gamma)\sqrt{T}}{\sqrt{\gamma(1 - \gamma)}}
\]
\(\bar{p}_G\) is the observed proportion of Green words in the sample, this rate is roughly controlled by how you set the watermarking strength (\(\delta\)).
In common settting we use the critial value of 3 (\(\tau\)) to determine if a text is watermarked or not.
We can plot how does \(\bar{p}_G\) vary with different sample sizes.

title: AI watermarks
text:
Preventing being flagged out

Watermark algorithms calculate probabilities based on preceding word sequences.
Merely replacing words with synonyms often preserves the underlying statistical graph.
Instead, restructure clauses/Splitting:

Break one long compound sentence into two punchy, short sentences.
Turn passive clauses into active personal statements (“The experiment was concluded” -> “We wrapped up the trials on Friday”).
Insert concrete examples, personal anecdotes, or unique domain terminology.

title: AI watermarks
text:
Cross-Model Paraphrasing

LLM1 -> “Watermarked” -> LLM2 -> “Unwatermarked”
Usually LLM2 will be some open-source model that is not watermarked, and it will paraphrase the text in a way that removes the watermark.
Laziest approach to avoid detection, but it can also introduce errors or change the meaning of the text.

title: AI watermarks
text:
Daily Life Implications








Scenario
Watermark Risk
Real-World Impact




Brainstorming & Outlining
Zero
Ideas, bullet points, and high-level concepts carry no sentence-level token distribution.


Proofreading / Polishing your own draft
Negligible
If the ideas and majority of words are yours, the AI merely fixes grammar or word order. There is very little AI token sequence for a detector to latch onto.


Direct Generation (Copy-Pasting full drafts)
High
The text contains raw, continuous model token sequences that reliably trigger detection algorithms.

title: AI watermarks
section: Does free online AI watermark detector and remover work?
text:
Does free online AI watermark detector and remover work?

Challenges for free detectors:

Getting the private key that generated the green/red split is impossible
Free detectors have to guess the watermarking strength and the green/red split.

Easy way for most free online AI watermark detector and remover tools:

Shallow heuristics or,
Simple statistical tests

title: AI watermarks
text:
Watermarks on other modality
Text watermarking is not the only modality that can be watermarked. Other modalities include:

Image watermarking

Well-established field,
Visible or hidden patterns embedded in the pixels of an image.

Audio watermarking

Similar to image watermarking, but applied to audio signals.
Adding low-level noise or frequency patterns


Still text watermarking is more challenging due to the discrete nature of language and the need for semantic coherence.

title: AI watermarks
text:
Takeaways

Simple paraphrasing or synonym replacement is not enough to remove watermarks.
Restructuring sentences, adding personal anecdotes, and using unique domain terminology are more effective strategies
Existing free online AI watermark detector and remover tools may not be reliable due to the lack of access to the private key and reliance on shallow heuristics or simple statistical tests.

title: AI watermarks
section: Open Discussion: The Future of Provenance
text:
Open Discussion: The Future of Provenance

Where is the line? If an AI polishes your original draft into its own green-list vocabulary, is that original work or AI ghostwriting?
The Enforcement Paradox: If tech-savvy users can easily wipe watermarks with open-source tools, who does watermarking actually protect?
The Keyholder Dilemma: Should tech companies keep watermark keys private, or should verification tools be open to certain level that public can verify it?

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
This week’s path

EHR — what is in the digital chart, and common data traps

Why regression — summarize “how \(y\) changes with \(x\)”

Diagnostics — check whether the line’s assumptions look reasonable

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Why fit a line? (intuition first)
Healthcare question: Does systolic blood pressure tend to rise with age?

Plot age (\(x\)) against blood pressure (\(y\)): points scatter, but often show an upward trend.
A best-fit line summarizes that trend: “on average, how does \(y\) change as \(x\) increases?”

In plain English

\(\beta_1\): average change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x\) (holding other predictors fixed, when there are several)
\(\beta_0\): predicted \(y\) when all predictors are zero (often not clinically meaningful; still needed mathematically)
\(\epsilon\): leftover person-to-person noise the line does not explain

We fit the line so we can describe, predict, and later test whether a relationship is compatible with chance.

title: EHR data and linear regression
section: Introduction to the Linear Regression Model
text:
Introduction to the Linear Regression Model
With that intuition, the linear regression model is formally defined as \[
\begin{aligned}
y_{i} = & \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1i} + \beta_{2}x_{2i} + \dots + \beta_{p}x_{pi} + \epsilon_{i} \text{, or}\\
\mathbb{y} = &\mathbb{\beta}\mathbb{X}+ \mathbb{\epsilon}
\end{aligned}
\]

Systematic part (predictors / independent variables)
Random part: individual outcomes vary by an error term \(\epsilon_{i}\)
It is assumed that \(\epsilon_{i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\epsilon}^{2})\)







Optional / advanced


The matrix form \(\mathbf{y}=\boldsymbol{\beta}\mathbf{X}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) is a compact way to write the same model for many predictors. Focus first on the scalar equation and the meaning of \(\beta\) and \(\epsilon\).

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Prediction in regression


Confidence Interval (CI) for the Mean Response: The average expected outcome for all individuals with a specific predictor value \(x\)

Uncertainty: Uncertainty on \(\mathbb{\beta}\)


Prediction Interval (PI) for a New Observation: Predict the specific outcome \(y\) for a single, new individual with a specific predictor value \(x\).

Uncertainty: Uncertainty on \(\mathbb{\beta}\) and Uncertainty on \(\mathbb{X}\)



import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm

# 1. Generate synthetic data
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.linspace(1, 10, 50)
# True relationship with some random noise
y = 3 * x + 10 + np.random.normal(0, 4, size=len(x))

# 2. Fit the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model
# statsmodels requires manually adding a constant for the intercept
X_with_const = sm.add_constant(x)
model = sm.OLS(y, X_with_const).fit()

# 3. Generate predictions and intervals
# get_prediction calculates standard errors for both the mean and new observations
predictions = model.get_prediction(X_with_const)
summary_frame = predictions.summary_frame(alpha=0.05) # 95% intervals

# Extract the calculated components
y_pred = summary_frame['mean']
ci_lower = summary_frame['mean_ci_lower']
ci_upper = summary_frame['mean_ci_upper']
pi_lower = summary_frame['obs_ci_lower']
pi_upper = summary_frame['obs_ci_upper']

# 4. Create the visualization
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))

# Plot the actual data points
ax.scatter(x, y, color='dodgerblue', alpha=0.7, label='Actual Data Points')

# Plot the regression line
ax.plot(x, y_pred, color='crimson', linewidth=2.5, label='Regression Line (Mean Response)')

# Plot the 95% Confidence Interval (CI)
ax.fill_between(x, ci_lower, ci_upper, color='crimson', alpha=0.3, 
                label='95% Confidence Interval (Uncertainty of the Line)')

# Plot the 95% Prediction Interval (PI)
ax.fill_between(x, pi_lower, pi_upper, color='gray', alpha=0.2, 
                label='95% Prediction Interval (Uncertainty of New Data)')

# Formatting the plot
ax.set_title('Confidence Interval vs. Prediction Interval in Linear Regression', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel('Predictor (X)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('Outcome (Y)', fontsize=12)
ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=11)
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Evaluating regression



\(y_i\): The actual observed value.
\(\hat{y}_i\): The predicted value on the regression line.
\(\bar{y}\): The mean of all observed \(y\) values.


import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Generate synthetic data
np.random.seed(2)
x = np.linspace(1, 10, 15)
y = 3 * x + 5 + np.random.normal(0, 2, size=len(x))

# 2. Calculate Mean and Regression Line
y_mean = np.mean(y)
coeffs = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
y_pred = np.polyval(coeffs, x)

# 3. Select the point furthest from the regression line for better visualization
# Using np.argmax to find the data point with the largest positive residual
idx = np.argmax(y - y_pred)
xi = x[idx]
yi = y[idx]
y_pred_i = y_pred[idx]

# 4. Create the plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))

# Plot data, mean line, and regression line
ax.scatter(x, y, color='dodgerblue', alpha=0.4, label='Data points')
ax.scatter(xi, yi, color='red', s=100, zorder=5, label='Highlighted Point ($y_i$)')
ax.axhline(y_mean, color='green', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label='Mean ($\overline{y}$)')
ax.plot(x, y_pred, color='darkorange', linewidth=2, label='Regression Line ($\hat{y}_i$)')

# Draw the decomposition lines for the highlighted point
# ESS component (Mean to Regression Line)
ax.annotate('', xy=(xi, y_pred_i), xytext=(xi, y_mean),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='<->', color='purple', lw=2.5))
ax.text(xi - 0.2, (y_pred_i + y_mean) / 2, 'Explained\n($\hat{y}_i - \overline{y}$)', 
        color='purple', ha='right', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# RSS component (Regression Line to Actual Point)
ax.annotate('', xy=(xi, yi), xytext=(xi, y_pred_i),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='<->', color='crimson', lw=2.5))
ax.text(xi - 0.2, (yi + y_pred_i) / 2, 'Residual\n($y_i - \hat{y}_i$)', 
        color='crimson', ha='right', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# TSS component (Bracket on the right side)
ax.annotate('', xy=(xi + 0.1, yi), xytext=(xi + 0.1, y_mean),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle=']-[, widthB=0.5, widthA=0.5', color='black', lw=1.5))
ax.text(xi + 0.3, (yi + y_mean) / 2, 'Total Deviation\n($y_i - \overline{y}$)', 
        color='black', ha='left', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# Formatting
ax.set_title('Decomposition of Total Deviation for a High-Residual Point', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel('X')
ax.set_ylabel('Y')
ax.legend(loc='upper left')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The following relationship holds \[TSS = ESS + RSS\] TSS (Total Sum of Squares): \[\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2\] ESS (Explained Sum of Squares): \[\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\] RSS (Residual Sum of Squares):\[\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
\(R^2\): The Coefficient of Determination

\(R^2\) is the percentage of variance explained by the linear model

\[
R^2 = \frac{ESS}{TSS} = 1 - \frac{RSS}{TSS}
\]

\(R^2 = 0\): the model explains none of the variance in the outcome (the regression line is flat at the mean, \(\bar{y}\)).
\(R^2 = 1\): the model explains 100% of the variance (every data point falls exactly on the regression line, meaning RSS is zero).

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Inference on linear model

Even if we have \(R^2\), we need to know whether the explained variance is statistically significant.
Null Hypothesis \[
H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_p = 0
\]
Test statistics

\[
F = \frac{ESS / df_{ESS}}{RSS / df_{RSS}} \sim F_{df_{ESS},df_{RSS}}
\]

\(df_{ESS} = p\) (the number of predictor variables)
\(df_{RSS} = n - (p + 1)\) (the number of observations minus the total number of estimated parameters, including the intercept)

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Inference on individual \(\beta_i\)

Investigate whether each predictor makes a statistically significant contribution to the outcome
Null Hypothesis \[
H_0: \beta_i = 0
\]
Test statistics

\[
\beta_i \sim t_{n-(p+1)}(0,\frac{s_{y\vert{}x}^{2}}{(n-1)s_{x_i}^{2}(1-r_{i}^{2})})
\]

Implication in linear model: Including other predictors to control for confounding commonly makes it more difficult to reject the null hypothesis
Some of the unadjusted association is explained by those other predictors.

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Assumption on linear regression
Ask these in everyday language first (formal names in parentheses):

Is the trend roughly a straight line? (Linearity)
Do leftovers look roughly bell-shaped? (Normality of errors)
Are leftovers independent (not clustered in time, space, or repeated measures)? (Independence of errors)
Is the leftover scatter similar at low and high fitted values? (Homoscedasticity / constant variance)
Are two predictors saying almost the same thing? (No multicollinearity)

Failure modes matter clinically: e.g. if sicker patients get more labs, associations estimated from complete cases can be biased.

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Linearity
Plain check: Does \(y\) change at a roughly constant rate as \(x\) increases, or is there a bend / threshold?
The model assumes that the outcome changes linearly with each continuous predictor.
Checking:

Residual versus Predictor (RVP) plots


import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Generate synthetic data with a THRESHOLD (piecewise linear) effect
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.random.uniform(0, 100, 300)

# Define a threshold at X = 50
threshold = 50
# The 'effect' is 0 before the threshold, and scales linearly after
spline_term = np.maximum(0, x - threshold)

# True relationship: flat before 50, positive slope after
y = 20 + 1.5 * spline_term + np.random.normal(0, 5, 300)

# 2. Fit the Misspecified Linear Model (ignoring the threshold)
X_linear = sm.add_constant(x)
model_linear = sm.OLS(y, X_linear).fit()
fitted_linear = model_linear.fittedvalues
residuals_linear = model_linear.resid

# 3. Fit the Correctly Specified Model (Piecewise / Linear Spline)
# The design matrix includes the constant, the base X, and the spline term
X_spline = np.column_stack((np.ones(len(x)), x, spline_term))
model_spline = sm.OLS(y, X_spline).fit()
fitted_spline = model_spline.fittedvalues
residuals_spline = model_spline.resid

# 4. Create the 1x3 Combined Visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

# --- Plot 1: Fitted Regression Lines vs. Observations ---
axes[0].scatter(x, y, color='dodgerblue', alpha=0.5, label='Observed Data')
sort_idx = np.argsort(x)

# Plot Misspecified Fit
axes[0].plot(x[sort_idx], fitted_linear[sort_idx], color='purple', 
             linewidth=3, linestyle='--', label='Misspecified (Strict Linear)')
# Plot Corrected Fit (Spline)
axes[0].plot(x[sort_idx], fitted_spline[sort_idx], color='crimson', 
             linewidth=3, label='Corrected (Linear Spline)')

axes[0].set_title('Outcome vs. Predictor', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Predictor ($X$)\n(e.g., Drug Dosage)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Outcome ($Y$)\n(e.g., Response Level)')
axes[0].legend()

# --- Plot 2: Residuals vs. Predictor (Misspecified) ---
sns.residplot(x=x, y=residuals_linear, lowess=True,
              line_kws={'color': 'purple', 'lw': 3, 'label': 'LOWESS Smooth'}, 
              scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.5, 'color': 'gray'}, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5)
axes[1].set_title('RVP: Misspecified Model', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Predictor ($X$)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Residuals')
axes[1].legend()

# --- Plot 3: Residuals vs. Predictor (Corrected) ---
sns.residplot(x=x, y=residuals_spline, lowess=True,
              line_kws={'color': 'green', 'lw': 3, 'label': 'LOWESS Smooth'}, 
              scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.5, 'color': 'gray'}, ax=axes[2])
axes[2].axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5)
axes[2].set_title('RVP: Corrected Model', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[2].set_xlabel('Predictor ($X$)')
axes[2].set_ylabel('Residuals')
axes[2].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Mitigation plan linearity

Categorize the continuous predictor.
The predictor has the threshold effect
Transformations to the predictor (e.g., adding quadratic terms, log transformations)
The predictor has the non-linear effect on the outcome
Piecewise Regression
Specifying a threshold point in the regression model

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Normality of Errors
Plain check: Do residuals look like a bell (symmetric pile around zero), or are they piled on one side / heavy-tailed?

\(\epsilon \text{i.i.d} N(0,1)\) is assumed
Normality checking with Q-Q plot:

Diagonal line: Normal
Upward curvature: Residuals are right-skewed (Floor effects of X).
Downward curvature: Residuals are left-skewed (Ceiling effects of X).



import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as stats
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Generate synthetic Count Data (Poisson process)
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.random.uniform(1, 8, 300)

# In a Poisson process, the rate (lambda) often grows exponentially
true_lambda = np.exp(0.5 * x)

# Generate counts based on the Poisson rate
# Counts are strictly non-negative integers (0, 1, 2, 3...)
y = np.random.poisson(true_lambda)

# 2. Fit a standard Linear Regression (OLS) ignoring the count nature of the data
X_with_const = sm.add_constant(x)
model = sm.OLS(y, X_with_const).fit()
residuals = model.resid
fitted = model.fittedvalues

# 3. Create the 1x3 Diagnostic Visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

# --- Plot 1: The Raw Data and OLS Fit ---
axes[0].scatter(x, y, color='dodgerblue', alpha=0.5, label='Count Data (Observed)')
sort_idx = np.argsort(x)
axes[0].plot(x[sort_idx], fitted[sort_idx], color='crimson', 
             linewidth=3, label='OLS Linear Fit')
axes[0].set_title('Count Outcome vs. Predictor', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Predictor ($X$)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Count Outcome ($Y$)')
axes[0].legend()

# --- Plot 2: Histogram of Residuals ---
sns.histplot(residuals, kde=True, ax=axes[1], color='purple', stat='density')
# Overlay a theoretical normal distribution for comparison
mu, std = stats.norm.fit(residuals)
xmin, xmax = axes[1].get_xlim()
x_pdf = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, 100)
p_pdf = stats.norm.pdf(x_pdf, mu, std)
axes[1].plot(x_pdf, p_pdf, 'k--', linewidth=2, label='Normal Reference')

axes[1].set_title('Histogram of Residuals', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Residuals')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Density')
axes[1].legend()

# --- Plot 3: Normal Q-Q Plot ---
# We use statsmodels' qqplot and draw a 45-degree reference line
sm.qqplot(residuals, line='45', fit=True, ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title('Normal Q-Q Plot', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Mitigation plan

Transforming the outcome variable (e.g., replacing \(y\) with \(log(y)\))
This could also imply other regression (i.e. Poisson, Negative-binomial regression)

title: EHR data and linear regression
text:
Independence of errors
Plain check: Is each leftover “its own story,” or are nearby / same-patient / same-clinic residuals similar?

\(\epsilon \text{ i.i.d} N(0,1)\) is assumed

Some obvious situations that violate this assumption

Repeated measures on the same person
Temporal or spatial patterns among observations

Checking the group difference

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Generate Data with Simpson's Paradox (Biomedical Context)
np.random.seed(42)
n_groups = 4
n_obs = 40

# Cell lines have increasing average X, but drastically decreasing baseline Y
group_x_means = [10, 20, 30, 40]
group_intercepts = [120, 80, 40, 0]
group_names = ['Cell Line A', 'Cell Line B', 'Cell Line C', 'Cell Line D']

data = []
for i in range(n_groups):
    x = np.random.normal(group_x_means[i], 3, n_obs)
    # The true within-group slope is POSITIVE (+2.5)
    y = group_intercepts[i] + 2.5 * x + np.random.normal(0, 5, n_obs)
    
    for j in range(n_obs):
        data.append([group_names[i], x[j], y[j]])

df = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=['Cell_Line', 'Protein_Expression', 'Growth_Rate'])

# 2. Fit the Misspecified OLS Model
X_ols = sm.add_constant(df['Protein_Expression'])
model_ols = sm.OLS(df['Growth_Rate'], X_ols).fit()
df['OLS_Fitted'] = model_ols.fittedvalues
df['OLS_Residuals'] = model_ols.resid

# 3. Fit the Correct Mixed-Effect Model
model_mixed = smf.mixedlm("Growth_Rate ~ Protein_Expression", df, groups=df["Cell_Line"]).fit()
df['Mixed_Fitted'] = model_mixed.fittedvalues

# 4. Create the 1x2 Combined Visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))

# --- Setup Explicit Color Mapping ---
unique_groups = sorted(df['Cell_Line'].unique())
palette = sns.color_palette('Set1', n_colors=len(unique_groups))
color_map = dict(zip(unique_groups, palette))

# --- Subplot 1: Model Fit Comparison (OLS vs. Mixed-Effect) ---
# Plot raw data colored by group using the explicit color map
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='Protein_Expression', y='Growth_Rate', 
                hue='Cell_Line', palette=color_map, s=60, alpha=0.5, ax=axes[0])

# Overlay the Misspecified OLS Line (Black, dashed)
sort_idx = np.argsort(df['Protein_Expression'].values)
axes[0].plot(df['Protein_Expression'].values[sort_idx], df['OLS_Fitted'].values[sort_idx], 
             color='black', linewidth=4, linestyle='--', label='Misspecified OLS Slope')

# Overlay the Corrected Mixed-Effect Lines (Solid, exactly matching scatter colors)
for name, group in df.groupby('Cell_Line'):
    sort_idx_g = np.argsort(group['Protein_Expression'].values)
    axes[0].plot(group['Protein_Expression'].values[sort_idx_g], 
                 group['Mixed_Fitted'].values[sort_idx_g], 
                 linewidth=3, color=color_map[name])

axes[0].set_title('Model Comparison: OLS vs. Mixed-Effect', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Predictor ($X$): Protein Expression')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Outcome ($Y$): Growth Rate')

# Adjust legend for Plot 1
handles, labels = axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
axes[0].legend(handles=handles, labels=labels, loc='upper right')

# --- Subplot 2: Diagnosing the Error (OLS Residuals colored by Group) ---
# We plot the OLS residuals against the OLS fitted values, also using the exact same colors
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='OLS_Fitted', y='OLS_Residuals', 
                hue='Cell_Line', palette=color_map, s=70, alpha=0.8, ax=axes[1])

# Add the standard zero reference line
axes[1].axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

axes[1].set_title('Diagnostic: OLS Residuals by Group', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Fitted Values ($\hat{y}$)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('OLS Residuals ($y - \hat{y}$)')

# Move legend outside the plot for cleaner viewing
axes[1].legend(title='Cell Line', bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

text:
Constant Variance (Homoscedasticity)
Plain check: Is the leftover scatter similar across the range of fitted values, or does it fan out like a funnel?



Constant variance of the error term, \(\sigma_{\epsilon}^{2}\) (violation = heteroscedasticity)
Impact: Precision of confidence intervals and P-values.
Checking: Residual versus Fitted (RVF) plots.
A horizontal funnel shape in these scatterplots is a signal of heteroscedasticity.
Having more observations won’t relieve the problem



import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Generate Synthetic Data with DECREASING Variance
np.random.seed(42)
practice_hours = np.random.uniform(10, 100, 300)

# The mean effect: More practice = faster completion time
true_mean_time = 120 - 0.8 * practice_hours

# The variance effect: More practice = less noise (higher consistency)
dynamic_std_dev = 35 - 0.3 * practice_hours 
true_variance = dynamic_std_dev ** 2

# Generate the outcome with the dynamic, non-constant noise
completion_time = true_mean_time + np.random.normal(0, dynamic_std_dev, 300)

# 2. Fit the Models
X_with_const = sm.add_constant(practice_hours)

# Model A: Misspecified OLS (Assumes constant variance)
model_ols = sm.OLS(completion_time, X_with_const).fit()

# Model B: Correctly Specified WLS (Weights = 1 / Variance)
weights = 1.0 / true_variance
model_wls = sm.WLS(completion_time, X_with_const, weights=weights).fit()

# 3. Structure Data for Seaborn 'hue'
# We build a long-format DataFrame combining both models
df_ols = pd.DataFrame({
    'Practice_Hours': practice_hours,
    'Completion_Time': completion_time,
    'Fitted': model_ols.fittedvalues,
    'Residuals': model_ols.resid,           # Raw errors
    'Model Specification': 'OLS (Misspecified)'
})

df_wls = pd.DataFrame({
    'Practice_Hours': practice_hours,
    'Completion_Time': completion_time,
    'Fitted': model_wls.fittedvalues,
    'Residuals': model_wls.resid_pearson,   # Weighted errors
    'Model Specification': 'WLS (Corrected)'
})

df_diagnostics = pd.concat([df_ols, df_wls])
color_palette = {'OLS (Misspecified)': 'crimson', 'WLS (Corrected)': 'teal'}

# 4. Create the Diagnostic Visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))

# --- Plot 1: Raw Data vs. Fitted Lines ---
# Plot raw observations once (using the OLS subset just to get the background dots)
sns.scatterplot(data=df_ols, x='Practice_Hours', y='Completion_Time', 
                color='lightgray', alpha=0.6, edgecolor='white', s=50, 
                label='Observed Performances', ax=axes[0])

# Plot both fitted lines using 'hue'
sns.lineplot(data=df_diagnostics, x='Practice_Hours', y='Fitted', 
             hue='Model Specification', palette=color_palette, 
             linewidth=3, ax=axes[0])

axes[0].set_title('Outcome vs. Predictor\n(Mean Fits)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Predictor ($X$): Hours of Practice')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Outcome ($Y$): Task Completion Time')

# --- Plot 2: Residuals vs. Fitted (RVF) ---
# Plot both sets of residuals using 'hue'
sns.scatterplot(data=df_diagnostics, x='Fitted', y='Residuals', 
                hue='Model Specification', palette=color_palette, 
                alpha=0.7, s=50, ax=axes[1])

axes[1].axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=2)
axes[1].set_title('Residuals vs. Fitted Values (RVF)\n(Raw vs. Weighted Errors)', 
                  fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Fitted Values ($\hat{y}$)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Residuals')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Generate Synthetic Data with MULTIPLICATIVE Seasonality
np.random.seed(42)
t = np.arange(1, 121)  # 120 months (10 years) of data

# The baseline trend grows steadily over time
trend = 10 + 1.5 * t

# The seasonal effect is a sine wave
seasonal_wave = 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12)

# MULTIPLICATIVE COMBINATION: 
# The amplitude of the season is multiplied by the growing trend
y_true = trend * (1 + seasonal_wave) + np.random.normal(0, 5, len(t))

# 2. Fit a Misspecified ADDITIVE Model
# We give the model the trend (t) and the seasonal shape (sin and cos), 
# but OLS will force them to have fixed, constant coefficients.
sin_t = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12)
cos_t = np.cos(2 * np.pi * t / 12)

# Design matrix: Constant, Time (Trend), and Seasonality
X = np.column_stack((t, sin_t, cos_t))
X_with_const = sm.add_constant(X)

model_additive = sm.OLS(y_true, X_with_const).fit()
fitted_additive = model_additive.fittedvalues
residuals = model_additive.resid

# 3. Create the Diagnostic Visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))

# --- Plot 1: Raw Data vs. Misspecified Additive Fit ---
axes[0].plot(t, y_true, color='dodgerblue', marker='o', markersize=4, 
             alpha=0.7, label='Observed (Multiplicative)')
axes[0].plot(t, fitted_additive, color='crimson', linewidth=3, 
             label='Misspecified Fit (Additive)')

axes[0].set_title('Outcome vs. Time\n(The Expanding Amplitude)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Time ($t$)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Outcome ($Y$)')
axes[0].legend(loc='upper left')

# --- Plot 2: Residuals vs. Time (Diagnosing Heteroscedasticity) ---
sns.scatterplot(x=t, y=residuals, color='gray', alpha=0.7, s=50, ax=axes[1])

# Add a LOWESS smooth to show the mean is roughly zero
sns.regplot(x=t, y=residuals, scatter=False, lowess=True, 
            line_kws={'color': 'purple', 'lw': 2, 'label': 'LOWESS Smooth'}, ax=axes[1])

# Draw a funnel shape to highlight the expanding variance
axes[1].plot([0, 120], [5, 45], color='red', linestyle=':', lw=2, label='Expanding Variance')
axes[1].plot([0, 120], [-5, -45], color='red', linestyle=':', lw=2)

axes[1].axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5)
axes[1].set_title('Residuals vs. Time\n(The "Funnel" Effect)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Time ($t$)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Residuals')
axes[1].legend(loc='upper left')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Generate Synthetic Data with MULTIPLICATIVE Seasonality
np.random.seed(42)
t = np.arange(1, 121)  # 120 months (10 years) of data

# The baseline trend grows steadily over time
trend = 10 + 1.5 * t

# The seasonal effect is a sine wave
seasonal_wave = 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12)

# MULTIPLICATIVE COMBINATION: 
# The amplitude of the season is multiplied by the growing trend
y_true = trend * (1 + seasonal_wave) + np.random.normal(0, 5, len(t))

# 2. Fit the Models
sin_t = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 12)
cos_t = np.cos(2 * np.pi * t / 12)

# Model A: Misspecified ADDITIVE Model (No interactions)
X_add = np.column_stack((t, sin_t, cos_t))
X_add_const = sm.add_constant(X_add)
model_additive = sm.OLS(y_true, X_add_const).fit()

# Model B: Correctly Specified MULTIPLICATIVE Model 
# We add interaction terms between Time (trend) and Seasonality
X_mult = np.column_stack((t, sin_t, cos_t, t * sin_t, t * cos_t))
X_mult_const = sm.add_constant(X_mult)
model_multiplicative = sm.OLS(y_true, X_mult_const).fit()

# 3. Structure Data for Seaborn 'hue'
df_add = pd.DataFrame({
    'Time': t,
    'Outcome': y_true,
    'Fitted': model_additive.fittedvalues,
    'Residuals': model_additive.resid,
    'Model Specification': 'Additive (Misspecified)'
})

df_mult = pd.DataFrame({
    'Time': t,
    'Outcome': y_true,
    'Fitted': model_multiplicative.fittedvalues,
    'Residuals': model_multiplicative.resid,
    'Model Specification': 'Multiplicative (Corrected)'
})

df_diagnostics = pd.concat([df_add, df_mult])
color_palette = {'Additive (Misspecified)': 'crimson', 'Multiplicative (Corrected)': 'teal'}

# 4. Create the 1x2 Diagnostic Visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))

# --- Plot 1: Raw Data vs. Fitted Lines ---
sns.scatterplot(data=df_add, x='Time', y='Outcome', color='lightgray', 
                alpha=0.6, edgecolor='white', s=40, 
                label='Observed Data', ax=axes[0])

sns.lineplot(data=df_diagnostics, x='Time', y='Fitted', 
             hue='Model Specification', palette=color_palette, 
             linewidth=2.5, ax=axes[0])

axes[0].set_title('Outcome vs. Time\n(Mean Fits)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Time ($t$)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Outcome ($Y$)')

# --- Plot 2: Residuals vs. Time (Diagnosing the Funnel) ---
sns.scatterplot(data=df_diagnostics, x='Time', y='Residuals', 
                hue='Model Specification', palette=color_palette, 
                alpha=0.7, s=50, ax=axes[1])

axes[1].axhline(0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=2)
axes[1].set_title('Residuals vs. Time\n(Raw vs. Corrected Errors)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Time ($t$)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Residuals')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

text:
Influential Points and Outliers
High leverage points are x-outliers with the potential to exert undue influence on regression coefficient estimates. Influential points are specific observations that have actually exerted an undue influence on the estimates. DFBETA statistics are recommended to quantify how much each coefficient would change if a specific observation were omitted from the dataset.

Code Illustrations: Python and R
Below are examples of how to fit a multiple linear regression model and generate the necessary diagnostic plots in both Python and R.

title: EHR data and linear regression

Python illustration

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as stats
import seaborn as sns

# 1. Generate Synthetic Data
np.random.seed(42)
x1 = np.random.normal(50, 10, 200)
x2 = np.random.normal(100, 20, 200)
# Create a continuous outcome with some normal noise
y = 15 + 2.5 * x1 - 1.2 * x2 + np.random.normal(0, 15, 200)

data = pd.DataFrame({'Y': y, 'X1': x1, 'X2': x2})

# 2. Fit the Linear Regression Model
X = sm.add_constant(data[['X1', 'X2']])
model = sm.OLS(data['Y'], X).fit()

# Print model summary (Contains F-test, R-squared, and coefficients)
print(model.summary())

# 3. Residual Diagnostics
residuals = model.resid
fitted = model.fittedvalues

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))

# A. Residuals vs Fitted (Checking Constant Variance / Homoscedasticity)
sns.residplot(x=fitted, y=residuals, lowess=True, ax=axes[0], line_kws={'color': 'red'})
axes[0].set_title('Residuals vs Fitted (RVF)')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Fitted Values')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Residuals')

# B. Normal Q-Q Plot (Checking Normality)
sm.qqplot(residuals, line='45', fit=True, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title('Normal Q-Q Plot')

# C. Residual Histogram (Checking Normality)
sns.histplot(residuals, kde=True, ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title('Residual Distribution')

plt.show()

title: Introduction to R
text:
A reminder: Variable assignment

Only I use <- to assign or update the value of a variable, then the variable will be updated to the new value.
Othersies you just do a calculation and the variable will not be updated.


# Assign the value '50' to the weight object.
weight <- 50
# Print out weight to the screen (50)
weight
# What's the value of weight plus 10?
weight + 10
# Weight is still 50
weight
# Weight is only modified if we *reassign* weight to the modified value
weight <- weight+10
# Weight is now 60
weight

title: Introduction to R
text:
Pipe operator |>
To prevent us from keep doing like a matryoshka doll

# Title: Nested function call example
# This shows the same work as a pipeline, but in nested form.
h(g(f(data_frame)))

R by default supports Pipe operator |> We can rewrite the above code as



# Pipe operator example
# Use the pipe operator to write the same 
# steps in a clearer, left-to-right order.
data_frame |> 
  f() |> 
  g() |> 
  h()



# This is the equivalent code of the left one.

data_frame <-f(data_frame)
data_frame <-g(data_frame)
data_frame <-h(data_frame)


‘|>’ takes the output from the left hand side and then pipes it to be the first argument of the right function.






Discussion question



What are the benefits of using pipe?

title: Practice Question 1
text:
1. Vector arithmetic and recycling
Before opening, the below experiement results has been recorded:

CD4: 12
CD8: 5
CD19: 35
CD56: 4


Scalar broadcasting vs. vector operations
Run the following chunk. You will use base_signals for the rest of this lab.









Add a 12.5% signal amplification (from a secondary antibody) to each marker’s base signal. Store the result in amplified_signals. The amplification rate is already given below.




















Over time, the signals naturally fade. Apply the fading rates in fade_rates to the base signals (not the amplified signals). Store the result in faded_signals.



















After you have created amplified_signals and faded_signals, run this chunk to build a data frame named signal_df:








Questions

What does R do when you multiply a vector of length 4 by a single number such as (1 + amp_rate) (a vector of length 1)?
Suppose you scramble the names of fade_rates to c(CD56 = 0.20, CD19 = 0.15, CD8 = 0.00, CD4 = 0.05) but leave base_signals in the original order. Do the usual arithmetic operators (*, +, …) match values by name or by position (1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd)?


Answer key

Recycling (often called broadcasting here). R has no separate scalar type: 1 + amp_rate is an atomic vector of length 1. R recycles that single value to length 4 so pairwise multiplication can run.
By position, not by name. Binary arithmetic ignores names. Index 1 multiplies with index 1, and so on. If fade_rates is reordered and base_signals is not, the wrong discount is applied. To align by name you would need something like fade_rates[names(base_signals)].




Indexing
Extract the Final_Signal column from signal_df. Hint: there are several valid approaches; try more than one.


















To read the cell in row 3, column 3, you can use either of these:








Questions

Compare signal_df[3, 3] with signal_df["CD19", "Final_Signal"]. Which is easier for another reader to understand without looking at the data?
Next month a student adds a column Sample_ID as column 1, so every later column shifts one place to the right. What would signal_df[, 3] refer to then, compared with signal_df[, "Final_Signal"]? Which is less sensitive to that change?
Compare the printed result and class() of signal_df$Final_Signal, signal_df["Final_Signal"], and signal_df[["Final_Signal"]]. Why does [ without a comma return a one-column data frame, while $ and [[ extract a numeric vector?


Answer key

signal_df["CD19", "Final_Signal"] is clearer: it names the row and the column.
After inserting Sample_ID at the front, signal_df[, 3] would be the old column 2 (Fade_Rate). signal_df[, "Final_Signal"] still means final signal no matter how many columns you add, so it is the more robust choice.
$ and [[ pull out the vector stored in that column. [ with no comma subsets the data frame as a list of columns, so signal_df["Final_Signal"] (and price_df[3] for the third column) stays a one-column data.frame.




Recycling rules and warnings
The core tests a background noise threshold correction on the four markers. Run the chunk below and inspect the output.








Questions

Why does adding noise_2 (length 2) to base_signals (length 4) run without a warning? What pattern of fees is applied to CD4, CD8, CD19, and CD56?
Why does adding noise_3 (length 3) warn, and what values does R actually add to the four items?
Why can “even” recycling (lengths that divide evenly) be more dangerous in an audit than the warning case?


Answer key

R recycles the shorter vector until it matches the longer one. When length(longer) %% length(shorter) == 0 (here \(4 \bmod 2 = 0\)), R treats the repeat as intentional and stays silent. The fees are \(+1, +2, +1, +2\).
\(4 \bmod 3 \neq 0\), so R still wraps around (the fourth item gets the first fee, \(+1\)) but warns: longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length.
If someone passed c(5, 0), R would add 5 to CD4 and CD9 and 0 to CD8 and CD56 with no warning. The code is valid, so the accounting error is easy to miss. The mismatched-length warning at least flags that something odd happened.




Finding help with ?
Inspect amplified_signals and round(amplified_signals):








Questions

Does round(amplified_signals) match what you expected? Hint: look at values that sit exactly on .5, then try a few extra examples of your own.
Type ?round in the console and read the Details section.

Which international standard does R follow?
How does that standard explain what you saw for round(amplified_signals)?



Answer key

Half-way cases do not always round “away from zero” or “always up”. They follow round half to even (the adjacent even integer).
IEC 60559 / IEEE 754. That is why a .5 can round up or down depending on whether the neighbouring integer is even.




Data types and coercion
During peak hours, a technician types "SATURATED" into the instrument log instead of 0 for a blank well:








Questions

What is the data type of "SATURATED" on its own?
After you build instrument_log as above, what is the data type of instrument_log[1]? Can you compute instrument_log[1] + instrument_log[3]?
What is R’s usual coercion hierarchy for atomic vectors (from most specific to most flexible)?


Answer key

Character.
Character as well — one character value forces the whole vector to character — so instrument_log[1] + instrument_log[3] is not valid numeric addition.
\[
\text{logical} \longrightarrow \text{integer} \longrightarrow \text{double (numeric)} \longrightarrow \text{character}
\]

title: Introduction to R
text:
R files
R code can be saved in a text file with the extension .R. You can then run the code in the R console or RStudio by sourcing the file using the source() function. For example, if you have a file named my_script.R, run it with source("my_script.R") in the R console.



Illustration of my_script.R in RStudio

title: Introduction to R
text:
Rmd/QMD files
You can save your R code in a file with the extension .Rmd or .qmd. This allows you to create dynamic documents that combine R code, text, and output. For example, the presentation slides are made from an improved version of .qmd.



Illustration of lecture slide (.qmd) in RStudio

title: Introduction to R
text:
RData files
You may save your data or functions to an .RData file and load it with load("PATH/TO/THE/DATA_FILE.RData").

RStudio may save your last working session, which can sometimes cause trouble.

Pro tips

Always clean up your environment when starting new work

title: Introduction to R
text:
Preface

You will encounter errors.
Getting an error in R is not a sign of failure;
it is simply R’s way of asking for clarification, or
The program is not designed to work in that way

title: Introduction to R
section: How to Read the Red Text Without Panicking
text:
How to Read the Red Text Without Panicking
When R throws red text at you, first determine what kind of message it is:

Message / Note: Just R talking to you (e.g., “The tidyverse packages have been loaded”). Action: Ignore.
Warning: The code did run, but something looks suspicious to R (e.g., Removed 5 rows containing missing values). Action: Read it, verify if it affects your analysis, but no immediate panic.
Error: The code stopped. R cannot proceed. Action: Time to debug.

title: Introduction to R
section: Identifying the key of the Error
text:
Identifying the key of the Error
Don’t read the whole error if it looks messy. Look for the recognizable words at the end of the message.
Common Biomedical Data Errors translated to plain English:

Error: object 'XXX' not found

Translation: You either haven’t run the line of code that creates/loads XXX yet, or you made a typo (e.g., you typed xxx).

Error in read_csv("FILE") : could not find function "read_csv"

Key: could not find function
Translation: You forgot to load the package! Run library(tidyverse) or library(readr) first.

Error: unexpected symbol in "ggplot(data = clinical_df aes(x = treatment))"

Key: unexpected symbol
Translation: You missed a comma.

title: Introduction to R
text:
The AI Lifeline
When the error is confusing, Large Language Models (LLMs) are your best teaching assistants. However, “Garbage In = Garbage Out.”
Bad example

My R code doesn’t work!!!!!

Asking right question
To get an immediate, accurate fix, always provide the AI with these three components:

The Goal: What you are trying to do (briefly).
The Code: The exact lines that failed.
The Error: The exact copy-pasted red text.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Some example:

Act as an expert R programmer
Goal: I am trying to [e.g., create a scatterplot of gene expression versus patient age using ggplot2].
Here is my code:
[Paste your code here]
Here is the error message I received:
[Paste the EXACT error message here]
Please tell me what went wrong and provide the corrected code.

title: Introduction to R
section: Part 3: Best Practices for AI-Assisted Coding
text:
Part 3: Best Practices for AI-Assisted Coding

Don’t just copy-paste the fix: Always read the AI’s explanation. If you just copy-paste, you will make the exact same error tomorrow. Ask yourself: “What was the key of my mistake?”
Watch out for Hallucinations: AI sometimes invents R functions that don’t exist. If the AI’s code throws a new error saying could not find function..., reply to the AI with that new error!
Protect Sensitive Data: NEVER paste real, identifiable patient data or confidential research results into LLM. If the AI asks to see your data structure, use str(your_data) or head(your_data) and mock up the values, or simply provide the column names.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Introduction to R
R is a programming language popular for statistical computing, elegant graphics, and genomic data analysis.
Features

Free and open-source software
Easy to get started for scientific computing

Slide conventions

Use code formatting for special terms and examples, such as This or This are code.


# This is a code chunk

title: Introduction to R
text:
Arithmetic operations
R provides many arithmetic and statistical operations like +, -, *, /, %%, and ^

# example of basic operation
2+2

[1] 4

5*3

[1] 15

10/3

[1] 3.333333

10%%3 # %% returns the remainder of the division

[1] 1

2^3 # ^ is the power operation

[1] 8

title: Introduction to R
text:
Variables
Variables store information. To save a value, assign it to a variable. The assignment operator in R is <-. Occasionally, you may also see = used for assignment, but <- is the preferred style in R.
\[
\small
\text{Variable <- Value}
\]
Benefits of using variables:

Store and manipulate data in a flexible way.
Make code more readable and maintainable.
Allow dynamic programming and automation.


# example of assigning variable called age

age <- 18
age

[1] 18

name <- "John"
name

[1] "John"

title: Introduction to R
text:
Naming conventions for variables
Variables can be called just about anything, but there are some rules in R:

Special characters like $, #, %, or spaces are not allowed.
A variable name must start with a letter or a dot (.), but if it starts with a dot, the next character cannot be a digit.
Variable names are case-sensitive (e.g., age, Age, and AGE are different variables).
You cannot use particular keywords such as TRUE, FALSE, if, else, or function as variable names as they are reserved for other purposes in R.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data types
Variables can store different types of data, and R has several built-in data types to support them. The data type of a variable determines what kind of values it can hold and what operations can be performed on it.
You can use the class() and typeof() functions to check the class and data type of any variable. R has five common data types:

Numeric
Integer
Complex
Logical
Character

title: Introduction to R
text:
Numeric (double)
The numeric data type is for numbers.

Can be whole numbers or decimals.
The default numeric type in R.
Stores values in double precision, so typeof() reports double.


# example of numeric type

height <- 1.70
height

[1] 1.7

class(height)

[1] "numeric"

typeof(height)

[1] "double"

title: Introduction to R
text:
Integer
The integer data type stores whole numbers.

Use the capital L suffix to create an integer value.
Convert a numeric value to integer using as.integer().
Convert an integer to numeric using as.numeric().


# example of integer type

siblings <- 2L
siblings 

[1] 2

typeof(siblings)

[1] "integer"

siblings <- as.numeric(siblings)
typeof(siblings)

[1] "double"

title: Introduction to R
text:
Logical
In R, the logical data type can be:

TRUE (carries a value of 1)
FALSE (carries a value of 0)

Tips: Logical values can behave like numbers. Numeric operations are possible on logical values, but use caution.

# example of logic type

male <- TRUE
male

[1] TRUE

typeof(male)

[1] "logical"

male <- male-1
male

[1] 0

typeof(male)

[1] "double"

title: Introduction to R
text:
Character
The character data type stores text strings, including letters, numbers, and symbols. Strings in R can be written with single or double quotes.

# example of character type

name <- "Ray"
name

[1] "Ray"

typeof(name)

[1] "character"

age <- "25"
age

[1] "25"

typeof(age)

[1] "character"

title: Introduction to R
text:
Comparison operations
Comparison operators compare two values and return a logical value TRUE or FALSE.

# example of basic operations
2 == 2 # Equal

[1] TRUE

5 < 3 # Less than

[1] FALSE

10 >= 3 # Greater than or equal to

[1] TRUE

10 != 3 # Not equal

[1] TRUE

## Weird behavior !!
1 == "1"

[1] TRUE

1 == TRUE

[1] TRUE

"1" == TRUE

[1] FALSE

title: Introduction to R
text:
Coercion
while performing any operations mixed with different data types in R, the values are automatically converted to the most general data type by coercion. The order is as below
\[

title: Introduction to R
text:
Functions
Functions are used to perform tasks on input values. For example, the sin() function calculates the sine of a number. The input to the function is given inside the parentheses.


\[
\sin (\pi) = 0
\]


# example of sin() function
sin(pi)

[1] 1.224606e-16




sin is the name of the function, and pi is the input. The output of the function is 0.
Why is the output not exactly 0? This is because π is stored as a double and is accurate to about 15–16 decimal places. As a result, sin(pi) is a very small number close to zero, but not exactly zero.

title: Introduction to R
text:
More function examples
Another example is floor(), which rounds a number down to the nearest whole number.

# example of floor(sin(pi)) function
sin_pi <- sin(pi)
floor(sin_pi)

[1] 0



The output of floor(sin(pi)) is 0. This is because the floor() function rounds down the value of sin(pi) to the nearest whole number.
R has many predefined functions, and you can also create your own functions. See the official documentation for more information.
Within RStudio, you can use ? to get help on a function. For example, ?floor gives information about the floor() function.

title: Introduction to R

You can customize functions in R to perform specific tasks. Benefits of using functions:

Make your code more organized and readable.
Allow for code reusability and modularity.

The format for writing a function in R is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\textit{function_name} &\leftarrow \text{function}(\textit{arguments}) \{ \\
& \textit{your code} \\
& \}
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Cancer cell population monitoring

Tumor evolution


Tumor grows and evolves under evolutionary pressure

Trophic

Immunological
Therapeutic


Intratumor heterogeneity (ITH): diversity in genetics, phenotype, or even epigenetic profiles among cells in the same tumor. That diversity can help some cells survive selection pressures.
Consequences of ITH

Therapeutic failure
Drug resistance





Intratumor heterogeneity of tumor cells from Walsh (n.d.)

title: Cancer cell population monitoring

ITH implies that tumor cells could (Darwinian):

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Preface

Predicting the population in the

microbiome
cells (tumors, donor-recipient interactions)


The idea of using these models is to estimate the potential growth of the cells of interest and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of growth.
The modeling techniques in this topic are largely borrowed from ecology, where the study of species populations is of crucial interest:

Interactions between species
Environment

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Simple model of tumor growth


A simple model to describe the change in a tumor cell population (\(\frac{dC}{dt}\)) is

\[
\frac{dC}{dt}=gC(t)-dC(t)=\alpha C(t)
\]


\(g\) is the growth rate of the tumor cells
\(d\) is the death rate of the tumor cells
\(\alpha\) is the net growth rate of the tumor cells









G



cell

cell



cell->cell


growth (g)



die

die



cell->die


death (d)

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Implication of the simple model



The population of the tumor cells at time \(t\) can be expressed as


\[
C(t) = C(0)e^{\alpha t}
\]



If \(\alpha > 0\), the population will grow exponentially.
If \(\alpha < 0\), the population will decline exponentially.
If \(\alpha = 0\), the population will remain constant.


Limitations

The model assumes that growth and death rates are constant over time, which may not be true in reality.
The model does not account for interactions with other cell types or the environment.
The model assumes there is no maximum population in a given environment.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Redesigning the model
From empirical observation, the growth of tumor cells usually follows these steps:

Starting rapid growth from a single/small collections of cells
The growth slows down as the population increases
Eventually, the population reaches a plateau

How to redesign the model

The growth rate is not constant; it is negatively proportional to the population size.
At a large enough population size, the growth rate will be zero.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Logistic growth model
An improved version of the simple model is the logistic growth model, which can be expressed as:

\[
\frac{dC}{dt}= \alpha(1-\frac{C(t)}{K}) C(t)
\]


\(K\) is the carrying capacity of the environment, which is the maximum population size that the environment can sustain.
\(\alpha\) is the intrinsic growth rate of the tumor cells.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Qualitative inspection


The analytical solution of the logistic growth model is

\[
C(t)=\frac{K}{1+\frac{K-C(0)}{C(0)}e^{-\alpha t}}
\]



\(C(t) < K\), the population will grow and reach the carrying capacity \(K\).
\(C(t) > K\), the population will decline and reach the carrying capacity \(K\).
\(C(t) = K\), the population will remain constant.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
What is missing?

The model does not account for interactions with other cell types or the environment.

Consider two populations with following interactions

Prey and predator

Predator population growth is positively affected by the prey population size
Prey population growth is negatively affected by the predator population size

Competition between two species


The growth of each species is negatively affected by the population size of the other species.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Lotka-Volterra competition model
Given two species, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in competition with each other, the competitive Lotka-Volterra model can be expressed as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dC_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 C_1(t) (1 - \frac{C_1(t) + \beta_{12} C_2(t)}{K_1}) \\
\frac{dC_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 C_2(t) (1 - \frac{C_2(t) + \beta_{21} C_1(t)}{K_2})
\end{aligned}
\]


\(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) are the intrinsic growth rates of species 1 and 2, respectively.
\(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are the carrying capacities of the environment for species 1 and 2, respectively.
\(\beta_{12}\) and \(\beta_{21}\) are the competition rates between species 1 and 2,

\(\beta_{12}\) represents the effect of species 2 on the growth of species 1.
\(\beta_{21}\) represents the effect of species 1 on the growth of species 2.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Lotka-Volterra prey-predator model
Given two species, \(C_1\) (prey) and \(C_2\) (predator), the prey-predator Lotka-Volterra model can be expressed as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dC_1}{dt} &= \alpha_1 C_1(t)(1 - \frac{C_1(t)}{K_1}) - \beta_{12} C_1(t) C_2(t) \\
\frac{dC_2}{dt} &= -\alpha_2 C_2(t) + \beta_{21} C_1(t) C_2(t)
\end{aligned}
\]


\(\alpha_1\) is the intrinsic growth rate of the prey population
\(\alpha_2\) is the intrinsic death rate of the predator population in the absence of prey.
\(\beta_{12}\) is the effect of the presence of predators on the prey death rate.
\(\beta_{21}\) is the effect of the presence of prey on the predator’s growth rate.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Qualitative inspection on ODEs

Systems of ODEs rarely have analytical solutions.
In many cases where ODEs do not have analytical solutions, we can use qualitative inspection to understand the behavior of the system.
Phase diagram: Plotting derivatives as an arrow field, which can provide insights into

the stability
behavior
Initial points

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Phase diagram

For a logistic growth model


\[
C(t)=\frac{K}{1+\frac{K-C(0)}{C(0)}e^{-\alpha t}}
\]

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Discussion on Lotka-Volterra competition model


We can find the equilibrium points of the system by setting \(\frac{dC_1}{dt} = 0\) and \(\frac{dC_2}{dt} = 0\), which gives us the following equations:

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1(t) &= K_1 - \beta_{12} C_2(t) \\
C_2(t) &= K_2 - \beta_{21} C_1(t) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

The intersection of these lines represents the equilibrium points of the system. (Detailed discussion can be found in McGehee and Mori (2024))

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Exclusion of one species


\(C_1\) wins

Condition: \(\beta_{12} < \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} > \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Species 1 exerts strong competitive pressure on Species 2 (\(\beta_{21}\) is large), while Species 2 exerts weak pressure on Species 1 (\(\beta_{12}\) is small).
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\) is a globally stable node.
\((0, K_2)\) is an unstable node.
\((0, 0)\) is an unstable saddle.



\(C_2\) wins

Condition: \(\beta_{12} > \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} < \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Species 2 exerts strong competitive pressure on Species 1 (\(\beta_{12}\) is large), whereas Species 1 exerts weak pressure on Species 2 (\(\beta_{21}\) is small).
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\) is an unstable node.
\((0, K_2)\) is a globally stable node.
\((0, 0)\) is an unstable saddle.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Bistability/Competitive Exclusion



Condition: \(\beta_{12} > \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} > \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Interspecific competition is stronger than intraspecific competition for both species. Each species inhibits the other more than it inhibits itself.
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\), \((0, K_2)\) are locally stable nodes.

The interior intersection point \((C_1^*, C_2^*)\) exists as a saddle












\[
C_1^* = \frac{K_1 - \beta_{12}K_2}{1 - \beta_{12}\beta_{21}}, \quad C_2^* = \frac{K_2 - \beta_{21}K_1}{1 - \beta_{12}\beta_{21}}
\] - Outcome: Priority Effect / Founders’ Advantage. The surviving species depends strictly on the initial condition.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Stable Coexistence



Condition: \(\beta_{12} < \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} < \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Intraspecific competition is stronger than interspecific competition for both species. Each population limits its own growth more than it limits the growth of its competitor.
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\), \((0, K_2)\) are unstable nodes.
The interior intersection point \((C_1^*, C_2^*)\) is a globally stable node.

text:
Preface
Before we really go into the modeling, we need to understand how to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in computer.


In mathematics

ODEs can be solved analytically (e.g., separation of variables, integrating factor, etc.)
If ODE does not have an analytical solution, mathematical techniques can be used to qualitatively analyze the behavior of the system (e.g., phase diagram, stability analysis, etc.)


In computer

ODEs can be solved numerically (Computer can only perform a finite number of calculations, so we need to approximate the solution at discrete time steps)
Numerical methods can be used to solve ODEs that do not have an analytical solution, or to simulate the behavior of a system over time.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
The Initial Value Problem (IVP)
We aim to solve an ordinary differential equation (ODE) of the form:
\[\frac{dy}{dt} = f(t, y), \quad y(t_0) = y_0\]

Analytical solutions are sometimes difficult or impossible to find for non-linear systems
Numerical methods approximate the solution at discrete time steps: \[t_0, t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n, t_{n+1}\]
Where \(h = t_{n+1} - t_n\) represents the step size.
Again, the computer can only perform a finite number of calculations, in any case computing the solution at discrete time steps is necessary.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Overview of Numerical Integration
The fundamental problem is to evaluate the integral over a single time step:
\[y(t_{n+1}) = y(t_n) + \int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} f(t, y(t)) \, dt\]
Numerical integration methods approximate the area under the curve \(f(t, y(t))\) using different strategies:
Where
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = f(t, y(t))
\]
Intuitively, we can think of \(f(t, y(t))\) as the slope of the solution curve at time \(t\). The integral represents the total change in \(y\) over the interval from \(t_n\) to \(t_{n+1}\).

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
section: Evaluating different methods of numerical integration
text:
Evaluating different methods of numerical integration
Imagine we are doing an integration like a Riemann sum. In a Riemann sum we assume \(dt\) is small enough to accurately approximate the area under the curve. In numeric integration, we need to consider how good is it.

Stability Error is bound and does not grow exponentially with time steps. Important for long-term simulations. (As an analogy in statistics, we want to make sure the estimator is consistent)
Accuracy The numerical methods should be close to the true solution.
Computational cost The method should be computationally efficient, especially for large systems or long simulations.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
section: The Simplest Method: Euler’s Forward Method
text:
The Simplest Method: Euler’s Forward Method
By approximating the derivative with a forward finite difference:
\[\frac{y_{n+1} - y_n}{h} \approx f(t_n, y_n)\]
We obtain the explicit Euler update rule:
\[y_{n+1} = y_n + h \cdot f(t_n, y_n)\]
Limitations

Demands very small \(h\) to avoid numerical divergence in dynamic systems.
Local Truncation Error (LTE): \(\mathcal{O}(h^2)\)
Global Truncation Error (GTE): \(\mathcal{O}(h)\) (First-order accurate)

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Runge-Kutta (RK) Methods

Core Idea: Instead of evaluating the derivative only at the beginning of the interval (\(t_n\)), evaluate \(f(t,y)\) at several carefully chosen intermediate trial points within \([t_n, t_{n+1}]\).
A weighted average of these intermediate slopes is used to compute the final step update.
Naming convention: \(RKX\) denotes a Runge-Kutta method that evaluates \(f(t,y)\) at \(X\) intermediate points.
e.g. Euler’s Method is simply a first-order Runge-Kutta method (\(RK1\)).



Developed around 1900 by Carl Runge and Martin Kutta, this family of methods improves accuracy without requiring higher-order derivatives of \(f(t,y)\).

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
The Classic RK4 Method
The most widely used explicit RK method balances computational cost and high accuracy. To step from \(y_n\) to \(y_{n+1}\), calculate four intermediate slopes:
\[\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= f(t_n, y_n) \\
k_2 &= f\left(t_n + \frac{h}{2}, y_n + h\frac{k_1}{2}\right) \\
k_3 &= f\left(t_n + \frac{h}{2}, y_n + h\frac{k_2}{2}\right) \\
k_4 &= f(t_n + h, y_n + h k_3)
\end{aligned}\]
Once the four slopes are computed, the next value is calculated via a weighted average resembling Simpson’s Rule:
\[y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{6} \left(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4\right)\]

text:

Geometric Intuition

\(k_1\) is the slope at the left boundary.
\(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are trial slopes at the midpoint.
\(k_4\) is a trial slope at the right boundary.


Error Properties

LTE: \(\mathcal{O}(h^5)\)
GTE: \(\mathcal{O}(h^4)\)
Order: \(4^{\text{th}}\)-Order accurate.

text:
Preface

Predicting the population in the

microbiome
cells (tumors, donor-recipient interactions)


The idea of using these models is to estimate the potential growth of the cells of interest and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of growth.
The modeling techniques in this topic are largely borrowed from ecology, where the study of species populations is of crucial interest:

Interactions between species
Environment

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Simple model of tumor growth


A simple model to describe the change in a tumor cell population (\(\frac{dC}{dt}\)) is

\[
\frac{dC}{dt}=gC(t)-dC(t)=\alpha C(t)
\]


\(g\) is the growth rate of the tumor cells
\(d\) is the death rate of the tumor cells
\(\alpha\) is the net growth rate of the tumor cells









G

cell->cell

cell->die


death (d)

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Implication of the simple model



The population of the tumor cells at time \(t\) can be expressed as


\[
C(t) = C(0)e^{\alpha t}
\]



If \(\alpha > 0\), the population will grow exponentially.
If \(\alpha < 0\), the population will decline exponentially.
If \(\alpha = 0\), the population will remain constant.


Limitations

The model assumes that growth and death rates are constant over time, which may not be true in reality.
The model does not account for interactions with other cell types or the environment.
The model assumes there is no maximum population in a given environment.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Redesigning the model
From empirical observation, the growth of tumor cells usually follows these steps:

Starting rapid growth from a single/small collections of cells
The growth slows down as the population increases
Eventually, the population reaches a plateau

How to redesign the model

The growth rate is not constant; it is negatively proportional to the population size.
At a large enough population size, the growth rate will be zero.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Logistic growth model
An improved version of the simple model is the logistic growth model, which can be expressed as:

\[
\frac{dC}{dt}= \alpha(1-\frac{C(t)}{K}) C(t)
\]


\(K\) is the carrying capacity of the environment, which is the maximum population size that the environment can sustain.
\(\alpha\) is the intrinsic growth rate of the tumor cells.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Qualitative inspection


The analytical solution of the logistic growth model is

\[
C(t)=\frac{K}{1+\frac{K-C(0)}{C(0)}e^{-\alpha t}}
\]



\(C(t) < K\), the population will grow and reach the carrying capacity \(K\).
\(C(t) > K\), the population will decline and reach the carrying capacity \(K\).
\(C(t) = K\), the population will remain constant.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
What is missing?

The model does not account for interactions with other cell types or the environment.

Consider two populations with following interactions

Prey and predator

Predator population growth is positively affected by the prey population size
Prey population growth is negatively affected by the predator population size

Competition between two species


The growth of each species is negatively affected by the population size of the other species.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Lotka-Volterra competition model
Given two species, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in competition with each other, the competitive Lotka-Volterra model can be expressed as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dC_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 C_1(t) (1 - \frac{C_1(t) + \beta_{12} C_2(t)}{K_1}) \\
\frac{dC_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 C_2(t) (1 - \frac{C_2(t) + \beta_{21} C_1(t)}{K_2})
\end{aligned}
\]


\(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) are the intrinsic growth rates of species 1 and 2, respectively.
\(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are the carrying capacities of the environment for species 1 and 2, respectively.
\(\beta_{12}\) and \(\beta_{21}\) are the competition rates between species 1 and 2,

\(\beta_{12}\) represents the effect of species 2 on the growth of species 1.
\(\beta_{21}\) represents the effect of species 1 on the growth of species 2.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Lotka-Volterra prey-predator model
Given two species, \(C_1\) (prey) and \(C_2\) (predator), the prey-predator Lotka-Volterra model can be expressed as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dC_1}{dt} &= \alpha_1 C_1(t)(1 - \frac{C_1(t)}{K_1}) - \beta_{12} C_1(t) C_2(t) \\
\frac{dC_2}{dt} &= -\alpha_2 C_2(t) + \beta_{21} C_1(t) C_2(t)
\end{aligned}
\]


\(\alpha_1\) is the intrinsic growth rate of the prey population
\(\alpha_2\) is the intrinsic death rate of the predator population in the absence of prey.
\(\beta_{12}\) is the effect of the presence of predators on the prey death rate.
\(\beta_{21}\) is the effect of the presence of prey on the predator’s growth rate.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Qualitative inspection on ODEs

Systems of ODEs rarely have analytical solutions.
In many cases where ODEs do not have analytical solutions, we can use qualitative inspection to understand the behavior of the system.
Phase diagram: Plotting derivatives as an arrow field, which can provide insights into

the stability
behavior
Initial points

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Phase diagram

For a logistic growth model


\[
C(t)=\frac{K}{1+\frac{K-C(0)}{C(0)}e^{-\alpha t}}
\]

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Discussion on Lotka-Volterra competition model


We can find the equilibrium points of the system by setting \(\frac{dC_1}{dt} = 0\) and \(\frac{dC_2}{dt} = 0\), which gives us the following equations:

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1(t) &= K_1 - \beta_{12} C_2(t) \\
C_2(t) &= K_2 - \beta_{21} C_1(t) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

The intersection of these lines represents the equilibrium points of the system. (Detailed discussion can be found in McGehee and Mori (2024))

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Exclusion of one species


\(C_1\) wins

Condition: \(\beta_{12} < \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} > \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Species 1 exerts strong competitive pressure on Species 2 (\(\beta_{21}\) is large), while Species 2 exerts weak pressure on Species 1 (\(\beta_{12}\) is small).
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\) is a globally stable node.
\((0, K_2)\) is an unstable node.
\((0, 0)\) is an unstable saddle.



\(C_2\) wins

Condition: \(\beta_{12} > \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} < \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Species 2 exerts strong competitive pressure on Species 1 (\(\beta_{12}\) is large), whereas Species 1 exerts weak pressure on Species 2 (\(\beta_{21}\) is small).
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\) is an unstable node.
\((0, K_2)\) is a globally stable node.
\((0, 0)\) is an unstable saddle.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Bistability/Competitive Exclusion



Condition: \(\beta_{12} > \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} > \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Interspecific competition is stronger than intraspecific competition for both species. Each species inhibits the other more than it inhibits itself.
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\), \((0, K_2)\) are locally stable nodes.

The interior intersection point \((C_1^*, C_2^*)\) exists as a saddle












\[
C_1^* = \frac{K_1 - \beta_{12}K_2}{1 - \beta_{12}\beta_{21}}, \quad C_2^* = \frac{K_2 - \beta_{21}K_1}{1 - \beta_{12}\beta_{21}}
\] - Outcome: Priority Effect / Founders’ Advantage. The surviving species depends strictly on the initial condition.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Stable Coexistence



Condition: \(\beta_{12} < \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} < \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Intraspecific competition is stronger than interspecific competition for both species. Each population limits its own growth more than it limits the growth of its competitor.
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\), \((0, K_2)\) are unstable nodes.
The interior intersection point \((C_1^*, C_2^*)\) is a globally stable node.

Outcome: Both species coexist indefinitely at reduced population levels relative to their single-species carrying capacities.

title: Regression diagnostics
text:
Overview of linear regression
In linear regression, our fundamental objective is to explain the variability observed in the outcome variable (\(Y\)) using one or more explanatory variable (\(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k\)).

\[
\hat{Y}_i = b_0 + b_1 X_{1i} + b_2 X_{2i} + \dots + b_k X_{ki}
\]

It is crucial to know

Does \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k\) really make explaination to \(Y\)
How good is the model performance?



(Note on terminology: In some literature, notably British and econometrics, SSR is termed “Explained Sum of Squares” (ESS) and SSE is termed “Residual Sum of Squares” (RSS). Always check definitions in your specific context).

title: Regression diagnostics
text:
Quick summary









Metric
Formula
Degrees of Freedom (\(df\))
Conceptual Intuition




SST
\(\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2\)
\(n - 1\)
Total variation in the outcome \(Y\) without using any predictors.


SSR
\(\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2\)
\(k\)
Variation accounted by the regression model.


SSE
\(\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2\)  \(= \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\)
\(n - k - 1\)
Unexplained variation; sum of squared discrepancies between observed points and regression surface.






\(n\) represents the sample size
\(k\) represents the number of predictors, excluding the intercept.

title: Regression diagnostics
text:
Goodness-of-Fit: \(R^2\)
\(R^2\) (The coefficient of determination) quantifies the proportion of total variation in the response variable explained by the linear combination of predictors:

\[
R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}
\]

Interpretation Rules

Range: In standard OLS with an intercept, \(0 \le R^2 \le 1\) (or \(0\%\) to \(100\%\)).
Interpretation: If \(R^2 = 0.74\), exactly 74% of the variability in \(Y\) is explained by the predictors included in the model, while the remaining 26% is attributable to residual noise or omitted factors.
Limitation: \(R^2\) is non-decreasing with respect to the addition of predictors. Adding completely unrelated random noise variables will force \(\text{SSE}\) to stay equal or decrease, artificially inflating \(R^2\).

title: Regression diagnostics
text:
Adjusted \(R^2\) (\(R^2_{\text{adj}}\))
The Adjusted \(R^2\) incorporates degrees of freedom to penalize excessive parameterization and prevent overfitting, :

\[
R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \left[ \frac{\text{SSE} / (n - k - 1)}{\text{SST} / (n - 1)} \right] = 1 - \left( \frac{\text{MSE}}{\text{MST}} \right)
\]

Alternatively expressed via \(R^2\): \[
R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1 - R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - k - 1}
\]
Key Properties

Increases only if a newly added predictor reduces \(\text{SSE}\) by a margin greater than what would be expected by pure chance.
Can occasionally yield a negative value when model fit is negligible; in such cases, it is effectively interpreted as zero.

title: Regression diagnostics
text:
\(F\)-Test for Model Significance
\(F\)-Test evaluates whether the collection of predictors collectively explains a statistically significant amount of variation.
Hypotheses

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): All slope coefficients are simultaneously zero.


\[
H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_k = 0
\]


Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): At least one slope coefficient is non-zero.


\[
H_1: \text{There is at least one} \beta_j \neq 0
\]

Difference on individual testing on \(\beta_i\)

\(\beta_i\) is a \(t\)-test
Repeated testing \(\beta_i\) cause p-value inflation
