title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Simple model of tumor growth


A simple model to describe the change in a tumor cell population (\(\frac{dC}{dt}\)) is

\[
\frac{dC}{dt}=gC(t)-dC(t)=\alpha C(t)
\]


\(g\) is the growth rate of the tumor cells
\(d\) is the death rate of the tumor cells
\(\alpha\) is the net growth rate of the tumor cells









G



cell

cell



cell->cell


growth (g)



die

die



cell->die


death (d)

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Implication of the simple model



The population of the tumor cells at time \(t\) can be expressed as


\[
C(t) = C(0)e^{\alpha t}
\]



If \(\alpha > 0\), the population will grow exponentially.
If \(\alpha < 0\), the population will decline exponentially.
If \(\alpha = 0\), the population will remain constant.


Limitations

The model assumes that growth and death rates are constant over time, which may not be true in reality.
The model does not account for interactions with other cell types or the environment.
The model assumes there is no maximum population in a given environment.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Redesigning the model
From empirical observation, the growth of tumor cells usually follows these steps:

Starting rapid growth from a single/small collections of cells
The growth slows down as the population increases
Eventually, the population reaches a plateau

How to redesign the model

The growth rate is not constant; it is negatively proportional to the population size.
At a large enough population size, the growth rate will be zero.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Logistic growth model
An improved version of the simple model is the logistic growth model, which can be expressed as:

\[
\frac{dC}{dt}= \alpha(1-\frac{C(t)}{K}) C(t)
\]


\(K\) is the carrying capacity of the environment, which is the maximum population size that the environment can sustain.
\(\alpha\) is the intrinsic growth rate of the tumor cells.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Qualitative inspection


The analytical solution of the logistic growth model is

\[
C(t)=\frac{K}{1+\frac{K-C(0)}{C(0)}e^{-\alpha t}}
\]



\(C(t) < K\), the population will grow and reach the carrying capacity \(K\).
\(C(t) > K\), the population will decline and reach the carrying capacity \(K\).
\(C(t) = K\), the population will remain constant.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
What is missing?

The model does not account for interactions with other cell types or the environment.

Consider two populations with following interactions

Prey and predator

Predator population growth is positively affected by the prey population size
Prey population growth is negatively affected by the predator population size

Competition between two species


The growth of each species is negatively affected by the population size of the other species.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Lotka-Volterra competition model
Given two species, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in competition with each other, the competitive Lotka-Volterra model can be expressed as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dC_1}{dt} = \alpha_1 C_1(t) (1 - \frac{C_1(t) + \beta_{12} C_2(t)}{K_1}) \\
\frac{dC_2}{dt} = \alpha_2 C_2(t) (1 - \frac{C_2(t) + \beta_{21} C_1(t)}{K_2})
\end{aligned}
\]


\(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) are the intrinsic growth rates of species 1 and 2, respectively.
\(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are the carrying capacities of the environment for species 1 and 2, respectively.
\(\beta_{12}\) and \(\beta_{21}\) are the competition rates between species 1 and 2,

\(\beta_{12}\) represents the effect of species 2 on the growth of species 1.
\(\beta_{21}\) represents the effect of species 1 on the growth of species 2.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Lotka-Volterra prey-predator model
Given two species, \(C_1\) (prey) and \(C_2\) (predator), the prey-predator Lotka-Volterra model can be expressed as

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dC_1}{dt} &= \alpha_1 C_1(t)(1 - \frac{C_1(t)}{K_1}) - \beta_{12} C_1(t) C_2(t) \\
\frac{dC_2}{dt} &= -\alpha_2 C_2(t) + \beta_{21} C_1(t) C_2(t)
\end{aligned}
\]


\(\alpha_1\) is the intrinsic growth rate of the prey population
\(\alpha_2\) is the intrinsic death rate of the predator population in the absence of prey.
\(\beta_{12}\) is the effect of the presence of predators on the prey death rate.
\(\beta_{21}\) is the effect of the presence of prey on the predator’s growth rate.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Qualitative inspection on ODEs

Systems of ODEs rarely have analytical solutions.
In many cases where ODEs do not have analytical solutions, we can use qualitative inspection to understand the behavior of the system.
Phase diagram: Plotting derivatives as an arrow field, which can provide insights into

the stability
behavior
Initial points

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Phase diagram

For a logistic growth model


\[
C(t)=\frac{K}{1+\frac{K-C(0)}{C(0)}e^{-\alpha t}}
\]

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Discussion on Lotka-Volterra competition model


We can find the equilibrium points of the system by setting \(\frac{dC_1}{dt} = 0\) and \(\frac{dC_2}{dt} = 0\), which gives us the following equations:

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1(t) &= K_1 - \beta_{12} C_2(t) \\
C_2(t) &= K_2 - \beta_{21} C_1(t) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

The intersection of these lines represents the equilibrium points of the system. (Detailed discussion can be found in McGehee and Mori (2024))

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Exclusion of one species


\(C_1\) wins

Condition: \(\beta_{12} < \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} > \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Species 1 exerts strong competitive pressure on Species 2 (\(\beta_{21}\) is large), while Species 2 exerts weak pressure on Species 1 (\(\beta_{12}\) is small).
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\) is a globally stable node.
\((0, K_2)\) is an unstable node.
\((0, 0)\) is an unstable saddle.



\(C_2\) wins

Condition: \(\beta_{12} > \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} < \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Species 2 exerts strong competitive pressure on Species 1 (\(\beta_{12}\) is large), whereas Species 1 exerts weak pressure on Species 2 (\(\beta_{21}\) is small).
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\) is an unstable node.
\((0, K_2)\) is a globally stable node.
\((0, 0)\) is an unstable saddle.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Bistability/Competitive Exclusion



Condition: \(\beta_{12} > \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} > \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Interspecific competition is stronger than intraspecific competition for both species. Each species inhibits the other more than it inhibits itself.
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\), \((0, K_2)\) are locally stable nodes.

The interior intersection point \((C_1^*, C_2^*)\) exists as a saddle












\[
C_1^* = \frac{K_1 - \beta_{12}K_2}{1 - \beta_{12}\beta_{21}}, \quad C_2^* = \frac{K_2 - \beta_{21}K_1}{1 - \beta_{12}\beta_{21}}
\] - Outcome: Priority Effect / Founders’ Advantage. The surviving species depends strictly on the initial condition.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Stable Coexistence



Condition: \(\beta_{12} < \frac{K_1}{K_2}\) and \(\beta_{21} < \frac{K_2}{K_1}\)
Mechanism: Intraspecific competition is stronger than interspecific competition for both species. Each population limits its own growth more than it limits the growth of its competitor.
Equilibria:

\((K_1, 0)\), \((0, K_2)\) are unstable nodes.
The interior intersection point \((C_1^*, C_2^*)\) is a globally stable node.

Outcome: Both species coexist indefinitely at reduced population levels relative to their single-species carrying capacities.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Preface
Before we really go into the modeling, we need to understand how to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in computer.


In mathematics

ODEs can be solved analytically (e.g., separation of variables, integrating factor, etc.)
If ODE does not have an analytical solution, mathematical techniques can be used to qualitatively analyze the behavior of the system (e.g., phase diagram, stability analysis, etc.)


In computer

ODEs can be solved numerically (Computer can only perform a finite number of calculations, so we need to approximate the solution at discrete time steps)
Numerical methods can be used to solve ODEs that do not have an analytical solution, or to simulate the behavior of a system over time.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
The Initial Value Problem (IVP)
We aim to solve an ordinary differential equation (ODE) of the form:
\[\frac{dy}{dt} = f(t, y), \quad y(t_0) = y_0\]

Analytical solutions are sometimes difficult or impossible to find for non-linear systems
Numerical methods approximate the solution at discrete time steps: \[t_0, t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n, t_{n+1}\]
Where \(h = t_{n+1} - t_n\) represents the step size.
Again, the computer can only perform a finite number of calculations, in any case computing the solution at discrete time steps is necessary.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Overview of Numerical Integration
The fundamental problem is to evaluate the integral over a single time step:
\[y(t_{n+1}) = y(t_n) + \int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} f(t, y(t)) \, dt\]
Numerical integration methods approximate the area under the curve \(f(t, y(t))\) using different strategies:
Where
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = f(t, y(t))
\]
Intuitively, we can think of \(f(t, y(t))\) as the slope of the solution curve at time \(t\). The integral represents the total change in \(y\) over the interval from \(t_n\) to \(t_{n+1}\).

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
section: Evaluating different methods of numerical integration
text:
Evaluating different methods of numerical integration
Imagine we are doing an integration like a Riemann sum. In a Riemann sum we assume \(dt\) is small enough to accurately approximate the area under the curve. In numeric integration, we need to consider how good is it.

Stability Error is bound and does not grow exponentially with time steps. Important for long-term simulations. (As an analogy in statistics, we want to make sure the estimator is consistent)
Accuracy The numerical methods should be close to the true solution.
Computational cost The method should be computationally efficient, especially for large systems or long simulations.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
section: The Simplest Method: Euler’s Forward Method
text:
The Simplest Method: Euler’s Forward Method
By approximating the derivative with a forward finite difference:
\[\frac{y_{n+1} - y_n}{h} \approx f(t_n, y_n)\]
We obtain the explicit Euler update rule:
\[y_{n+1} = y_n + h \cdot f(t_n, y_n)\]
Limitations

Demands very small \(h\) to avoid numerical divergence in dynamic systems.
Local Truncation Error (LTE): \(\mathcal{O}(h^2)\)
Global Truncation Error (GTE): \(\mathcal{O}(h)\) (First-order accurate)

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Runge-Kutta (RK) Methods

Core Idea: Instead of evaluating the derivative only at the beginning of the interval (\(t_n\)), evaluate \(f(t,y)\) at several carefully chosen intermediate trial points within \([t_n, t_{n+1}]\).
A weighted average of these intermediate slopes is used to compute the final step update.
Naming convention: \(RKX\) denotes a Runge-Kutta method that evaluates \(f(t,y)\) at \(X\) intermediate points.
e.g. Euler’s Method is simply a first-order Runge-Kutta method (\(RK1\)).



Developed around 1900 by Carl Runge and Martin Kutta, this family of methods improves accuracy without requiring higher-order derivatives of \(f(t,y)\).

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
The Classic RK4 Method
The most widely used explicit RK method balances computational cost and high accuracy. To step from \(y_n\) to \(y_{n+1}\), calculate four intermediate slopes:
\[\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= f(t_n, y_n) \\
k_2 &= f\left(t_n + \frac{h}{2}, y_n + h\frac{k_1}{2}\right) \\
k_3 &= f\left(t_n + \frac{h}{2}, y_n + h\frac{k_2}{2}\right) \\
k_4 &= f(t_n + h, y_n + h k_3)
\end{aligned}\]
Once the four slopes are computed, the next value is calculated via a weighted average resembling Simpson’s Rule:
\[y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{6} \left(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4\right)\]

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
The RK4 Update Rule


Geometric Intuition

\(k_1\) is the slope at the left boundary.
\(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are trial slopes at the midpoint.
\(k_4\) is a trial slope at the right boundary.


Error Properties

LTE: \(\mathcal{O}(h^5)\)
GTE: \(\mathcal{O}(h^4)\)
Order: \(4^{\text{th}}\)-Order accurate.

title: Cancer cell population monitoring
text:
Explicit vs Implicit Methods


Explicit Methods
Evaluate \(f(t,y)\) at known, previous time steps. Easy to compute but require small step sizes for stability.

Implicit Methods
Evaluate \(f(t,y)\) involving the unknown future state \(y_{n+1}\). Computationally intensive but highly stable for stiff equations.

WHO Observatory
The Global Health Observatory (GHO) is the World Health Organization’s (WHO) dedicated platform designed to enable users to explore a vast array of health data from around the world. Its primary purpose is to provide accessible, comprehensive insights into health-related indicators and country-specific data, supporting informed decision-making in global public health.
Key features include an extensive collection of health indicators, and detailed country profiles. The platform covers many general health indicators including mortality and burden of diseases, the Millennium Development Goals (child nutrition, child health, maternal and reproductive health, immunization, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, neglected diseases, water and sanitation), non-communicable diseases and risk factors, epidemic-prone diseases, health systems, environmental health, violence and injuries, and equity among others.

title: Creating Health Informatics Dashboard
section: Why an excel file is not enough
text:
Why an excel file is not enough








Criterion
Flat Denormalized Tables (e.g., Wide Excel / CSV)
Normalized Relational / Star Schema (WHO GHO Model)




Data Integrity & Consistency
Low: Country names, codes, and region tags are duplicated on every row. Vulnerable to spelling variations (e.g., “Swaziland” vs. “Eswatini”), update anomalies, and orphan records.
High: Country attributes reside in a single row inside RegionCountry. Updating an official country name or regional boundary requires modifying only one record without touching millions of historical indicator rows.


Storage Efficiency
Poor: Storing long text strings (e.g., “United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland”) repeated across hundreds of indicators and decades creates massive data bloat.
Optimal: Indicator tables store compact keys (e.g., 3-character ISO strings or integer IDs) alongside numeric values, minimizing disk footprint and memory bandwidth.


Query & Aggregation Optimization
Rigid / Slow at Scale: Adding a new health indicator requires modifying the entire table schema (adding columns) or stacking incompatible formats. Broad aggregation queries scan large amounts of redundant text.
Fast & Modular: Fact tables are append-only. New indicators exist as independent tables that link dynamically via existing dimension keys (Spatial Dim, Time Dim). Analytical engines only scan the specific columns requested by the user.


Sparse Matrix Handling
Inefficient: Indicators measured irregularly (e.g., every 3–5 years) force flat tables to store vast expanses of NULL or empty cells across millions of combinations.
Compact: If a country did not collect a specific metric in a given year, no row is inserted into that indicator’s fact table, preventing unnecessary overhead.









Exercise questions



Scenario: In 2018, the Kingdom of Swaziland officially changed its name to the Kingdom of Eswatini. What will be the impact for using Excel to store the data compare with the GHO model








Suggested Answers





In a flat spreadsheet: An analyst must run a batch search-and-replace across millions of historical rows spanning dozens of indicators. If an error occurs, historical records for “Swaziland” and modern records for “Eswatini” will fragment into two separate entities, breaking longitudinal trend lines.
In the WHO GHO schema: The fact records remain unchanged because the spatial key (e.g., ISO code SWZ) remains constant. Only one entry in the RegionCountry dimension table is updated: Country Name = “Eswatini”. Every connected visualization in Tableau immediately updates without altering the underlying observational facts.

text:
Modern data warehouse
In most of the data warehouses and business intelligence systems context, we will divide table into

Fact tables (quantitative health observations)

Contents: Numerical measurements + foreign keys that link to dimension tables
Structure: Narrow and very tall

Dimension tables (the context surrounding those observations).

Contents: Textual attributes, labels, categories, and a primary key (often a surrogate integer ID)
Structure: Short and wide (many descriptive columns, fewer total rows)

Primary key: the official ID card for a row in a table.
Foreign keys: Stores the exact primary key value from another table









Feature

Foreign Key (FK)




Primary Purpose
Uniquely identifies a row in its own table
Links to a primary key in another table


Null Values
Not allowed (Must have a value)
Allowed (Can be blank or null)


Duplicates
Not allowed (Every value is unique)
Allowed (Repeats across many rows)


Where it lives
Dimension tables (e.g., Spatial Dim in RegionCountry)
Fact tables (e.g., Spatial Dim in HIV_0000000001)

        - Time Dim (FK)

RegionCountry is a dimension table. HIV_0000000001 and others are fact tables

text:
Concept Deep Dive: Mackinlay’s Ranking of Visual Encodings
In 1986, computer scientist Jock Mackinlay extended Jacques Bertin’s semiology of graphics to develop an automated design theory for graphical presentations. His framework evaluates visual presentations using two foundational criteria:

Expressiveness: A visual encoding is expressive if and only if it communicates all of the intended information, and none of the false or unintended information.
Effectiveness: A visual encoding is effective if it exploits the capabilities of the human visual system to decode the data with maximum accuracy, minimal cognitive effort, and lowest error rate.

Mackinlay Ranking & Perceptual Assessment
Design Implication




Comorbidity Scatter Plot (TB vs. HIV)
Position on Common Scale (\(X\) and \(Y\) coordinates)
Rank 1 for Quantitative: The human visual system evaluates Cartesian positions with the highest mathematical accuracy.
Ideal for detecting correlations, clusters, and regression slopes without distortion.


Temporal Dual-Axis Trend (HIV Cases over Time)
Position / Slope, differentiated by Color Hue
Rank 1 (Position) for values; Rank 3 (Hue) for categories: The position along the shared temporal \(X\)-axis decodes rate of change accurately. Hue separates the two metrics without cognitive interference.
Ensures rapid interpretation of trends, though dual axes must maintain synchronized or clearly separated zero baselines to avoid misleading slope comparisons.


Global Choropleth Map (New HIV Cases)
Color Saturation / Luminance overlaid on Geographic Area
Rank 7/8 (Color) and Rank 5/10 (Area): Lower perceptual accuracy than position. Area acts as a confounding variable because large landmasses visually dominate irrespective of disease burden.
Effective for macro spatial patterns and geographic orientation, but poor for precision comparisons between countries.

title: Creating Health Informatics Dashboard
text:
Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)

Definition: The probability of an observation being missing is entirely independent of both observed variables and unobserved patient/national status.
Example: A rural clinic’s physical logbooks or electronic records are destroyed by an unforeseen localized flood. The missing reports bear no mathematical relationship to actual local HIV or TB infection rates.
Analytical Impact: While statistical power is reduced, simply dropping these records generally does not systematically bias point estimates.

title: Creating Health Informatics Dashboard
text:
Missing at Random (MAR)

Definition: Missingness depends systematically on observed covariates (e.g., national wealth, healthcare infrastructure tier) but not on the missing value itself once those covariates are controlled for.
Example: Lower-Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) with lower gross domestic product per capita frequently report HIV incidence or ART coverage every three to five years rather than annually, primarily due to the logistics and recurring costs of national biomarker surveys.
Analytical Impact: Dropping these records induces reporting bias unless adjusted via statistical weighting, imputation models, or stratifying by development index.

title: Creating Health Informatics Dashboard
section: Missing Not at Random (MNAR) — The Informative Null
text:
Missing Not at Random (MNAR) — The Informative Null

Definition: Missingness directly relates to the unobserved value itself, or to latent variables such as political censorship and social stigma.
Example: A jurisdiction omits or halts reporting on new HIV transmissions or key high-risk demographics specifically during an uncontrolled surge in infections to avoid international economic sanctions or political embarrassment. Alternatively, criminalization and societal stigma prevent marginalized populations from accessing diagnostic testing entirely.
Analytical Impact: Filtering out NULL values here creates an artificial illusion of public health success. The missing data points are systematically worse than the reported data points.

title: Creating Health Informatics Dashboard
text:
Surveillance Pitfalls & Misinterpretations
Clinical Enrollment Truncation: In regions with constrained diagnostic capacity or decentralized primary care, individuals with severe, rapid disease progression (such as untreated opportunistic infections or fulminant drug-resistant TB) often die before reaching a testing facility. Consequently, national clinical cohorts (HIV_ARTCOVERAGE) inadvertently sample patients with slower-progressing disease or better baseline access to health services.
The “Rising Prevalence Paradox”:When ART coverage expands significantly within a country, the total number of people living with HIV (HIV_0000000001) often increases rather than decreases over time. An untrained dashboard user might view a rising curve as an operational failure. In reality, broader ART coverage prevents premature mortality, transforming a fatal infection into a chronic manageable condition. Patients survive longer within the cohort, causing prevalence to accumulate even as newly acquired incident cases (HIV_0000000026) decline.
The Ecological Fallacy in Macro Visualizations The Ecological Fallacy occurs when an analyst infers individual-level clinical causality from aggregated national data.
For instance, plotting national HIV prevalence against national TB incidence and observing a positive regression slope does not prove that every HIV patient is contracting TB[cite: 8]. The two epidemics could be clustered in entirely different sub-populations within the same nation (e.g., HIV in urban transport hubs vs. TB in rural mines). Biological comorbidity must be validated via patient-level clinical studies, not assumed solely from macro correlations on a dashboard.

What is Differential Expression?
Every cell in your body has the same DNA, but different cells use different parts of that DNA to do their jobs. Gene expression is the process where a gene is turned “on” to make proteins that keep the cell running.
Differential expression simply means comparing how active genes are in two different conditions—for example, comparing healthy tissue versus diseased tissue, or treated cells versus untreated cells.
If a gene produces more copies in the diseased state, it is up-regulated. If it produces fewer, it is down-regulated.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Quick review
A hypothesis test asks: if there were truly no difference (or no effect), how surprising is the pattern we see in the data?

We state a skeptical null (\(H_0\)) and an alternative (\(H_a\)).
A small \(p\)-value means “this extreme a result would be unusual under \(H_0\)” — not “the hypothesis is proven.”

Why pairing matters here

Each cross- and self-pollinated plant shared a pot (same soil, water, light).
Comparing within pairs removes that shared environment; treating all plants as independent ignores it.

Keep that story in mind for the next two slides (wrong vs right test).

title: Introduction to R
text:
Wrong Approach: Independent t-test
We have 32 plants in total. Let’s see what happens if we adopt Darwin’s way’ (i.e. wrong statistical test). If we forget that the plants were grown in pairs (sharing the same pot), we might mistakenly assume we have two completely independent groups of 16 plants.


The Wrong Approach: Independent t-test
Hypothesis:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_0: & \mu_{\text{cross}} \leq \mu_{\text{self}} \\
H_a: & \mu_{\text{cross}} > \mu_{\text{self}}
\end{aligned}
\]


# INCORRECT: Running an unpaired 
# (independent) t-test
t.test(zea_mays$Cross_fertilized_plant, 
       zea_mays$Self_fertilized_plant, 
       alternative = "greater",
       paired = FALSE)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  zea_mays$Cross_fertilized_plant and zea_mays$Self_fertilized_plant
t = 1.406, df = 27.048, p-value = 0.08555
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is greater than 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.5046025        Inf
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
 19.11406  16.72656

title: Introduction to R
text:
Right Approach: Paired t-test


The problem with Darwin’s fallacy is that

Zea mays in the same pot shared

Same nutrient
Same weather condition


Violating the independent sample assumption of t-test. The corrected way is proposed by Ronald Fisher
Hypothesis:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_0: &  \mu_{\text{diff}} \leq 0 \\
H_a: & \mu_{\text{diff}} > 0
\end{aligned}
\]


# CORRECT: Running a paired t-test
t.test(zea_mays$Cross_fertilized_plant, 
       zea_mays$Self_fertilized_plant, 
       alternative = "greater",
       paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  zea_mays$Cross_fertilized_plant and zea_mays$Self_fertilized_plant
t = 2.0549, df = 15, p-value = 0.02887
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is greater than 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.3507378       Inf
sample estimates:
mean difference 
         2.3875

Health Insurance Claims Data
The Claims Lifecycle

Patient Encounter: Patient receives care (inpatient admission, outpatient clinic visit, or pharmacy fill).
Medical Coding: Medical coders translate clinical documentation into standardized billing codes (ICD for diagnoses, CPT/HCPCS for procedures, NDC for prescription drugs).
Claim Submission: The provider submits a claim form
Adjudication: The payer evaluates the claim against the patient’s coverage policy, determines negotiated rates, calculates patient cost-sharing and issues payment.

title: Large-scale healthcare datasets
text:
What is an EHR?
An Electronic Health Record (EHR) is the digital chart of a patient’s encounters with the health system—visits, diagnoses, labs, prescriptions, and clinical notes stored so clinicians (and later analysts) can reuse them.
Toy timeline (one patient):

Visit the clinic → demographics recorded

Doctor records a diagnosis → coded (e.g. ICD)

Lab is ordered → result coded (e.g. LOINC)

Prescription is filled → drug coded (e.g. ATC / RxNorm)

Coding systems are a shared language so different hospitals and software can mean the same clinical idea.

title: Large-scale healthcare datasets
text:
Components in EHR System

Demographics & Social Determinants: Age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic indicators.
Clinical Encounters & Diagnoses: Coded using international diagnostic standards:

ICD-9 / ICD-10 / ICD-11: International Classification of Diseases.

SNOMED-CT: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine for clinical concepts.


Prescriptions & Pharmacy Records: Coded using ATC or RxNorm frameworks.

Laboratory & Diagnostic Results: Coded using LOINC standards.
Unstructured Clinical Text: Progress notes, discharge summaries, radiological reports.

Poisson Regression (Directly Estimating RR)

Estimate Relative Risk with covariate adjustment through Poisson regression

\[
\ln(P(Y =  1 \mid X)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Exposure} + \sum \beta_k X_k

Exponentiating \(\beta_1\) yields the Relative Risk:
\[
\text{RR} = e^{\beta_1}
\]

title: Study design
text:
OR approximate to RR
Let’s recall the formulas using our \(2 \times 2\) table counts (\(a\) = Exposed Cases, \(b\) = Exposed Controls, \(c\) = Unexposed Cases, \(d\) = Unexposed Controls).


Relative Risk (RR): \[
\small
RR = \frac{\text{Risk in Exposed}}{\text{Risk in Unexposed}} = \frac{\frac{a}{a+b}}{\frac{c}{c+d}}
\]

Odds Ratio (OR):
\[
\small
OR = \frac{\text{Odds in Exposed}}{\text{Odds in Unexposed}} = \frac{\frac{a}{b}}{\frac{c}{d}} = \frac{a \times d}{b \times c}
\]

If a disease is extremely rare (e.g., 1 in 10,000 people), the number of sick (\(a\) and \(c\)) is incredibly tiny compared to the healthy people (\(b\) and \(d\)).
If \(a\) is vanishingly small, then adding it to \(b\) barely changes anything. Therefore the following approximation holds \[
\small
\begin{aligned}
a \ll b \implies & a + b \approx b \\
c \ll d \implies & c + d \approx d
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Network science
text:
What is Network Science?

Definition: An interdisciplinary field studying the topology, dynamics, and interactions of complex systems through graph theory.
Focuses on organizing principles across diverse domains without requiring advanced pure mathematics or algorithms.




Foundational Literature:

Barabási (2013), Network Science
Newman (2018), Networks
Menczer, Fortunato, and Davis (2020), A First Course in Network Science

title: Network science
text:
Mathematical Formalism
A network is mathematically defined as a graph \(G = (V, E)\):

Vertex / Node Set: \(V = \{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_N\}\), where \(|V| = N\) is the network size.
Edge / Link Set: \(E = \{(u, v) \mid u, v \in V\}\), where \(|E| = M\) is the total edge count.







Notation


In directed graphs, an edge \(e = (u, v)\) points from source \(u\) to target \(v\) (often termed a directed arc).

title: Network science
text:
Adjacency Matrix Representation
A graph \(G\) with \(N\) vertices is represented by an \(N \times N\) adjacency matrix \(A\):
\[
A_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } (i, j) \in E \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]



Undirected Networks:

Symmetric: \(A_{ij} = A_{ji}\)
Reciprocal interaction

Directed Networks:

Asymmetric: \(A_{ij} \neq A_{ji}\)
\(A_{ij} = 1 \implies i \to j\)




Weighted Networks:

Entries \(W_{ij} \in \mathbb{R}\) quantify tie strength, traffic, or frequency.

Unweighted Networks:

Entries are strictly binary \(A_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\).

title: Network science
text:
Eigenvector Centrality

Concept: A node is influential if it is connected to other highly influential nodes (recursive importance).
Mathematical Definition: \[
\lambda x_i = \sum_{j=1}^{N} A_{ij} x_j \iff A x = \lambda x
\]
By the Perron–Frobenius theorem, for a non-negative, irreducible matrix \(A\), the dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) corresponds to an eigenvector \(x^*\) whose entries are all non-negative (\(x_i \ge 0\)).
\(x_i^*\) represents the eigenvector centrality score of node \(i\).

title: Network science
text:
Empirical Example: Lifespan Risk Trajectories



Hsu et al. (2023) mapped risk factors and triggers across different age cohorts.
Eigenvector centrality identifies which psychological and environmental stressors act as core drivers across developmental stages.

title: Network science
text:
Betweenness Centrality

Concept: Measures how often a node falls on the shortest path (geodesic) between other pairs of nodes—acting as a bridge or gatekeeper.

\[
C_B(i) = \sum_{s \neq i \neq t \in V} \frac{\sigma_{st}(i)}{\sigma_{st}}
\]

\(\sigma_{st}\): Total number of shortest paths between node \(s\) and node \(t\).
\(\sigma_{st}(i)\): Number of those shortest paths passing through node \(i\).
Applications: Information brokerage (Burt’s structural holes), organizational gatekeeping, viral super-spreaders in epidemiological models.

title: Network science
text:
Community Detection vs. Clustering

Local Clustering: Evaluates local connectivity density—specifically, the probability that two neighbors of a node are themselves linked.
Community Detection: Partitions the network into modular sub-units with dense internal connections and sparse inter-group connections.










Political polarization in co-purchasing networks










Flavor pairing communities Ahn et al. (2011)

title: Network science
text:
Local Clustering Coefficient
The clustering coefficient \(C_i\) of node \(i\) measures the proportion of realized ties among its \(k_i\) neighbors:
\[
C_i = \frac{2 L_i}{k_i(k_i - 1)}
\]

\(L_i\): Number of links between neighbors of node \(i\).
\(\frac{k_i(k_i-1)}{2}\): Maximum possible links among \(k_i\) neighbors.
Average Clustering Coefficient: \[
\langle C \rangle = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} C_i
\]

title: Network science
text:
Homophily & Group Boundaries

“Birds of a feather flock together”


Definition: Tendency of nodes to form ties with similar others (based on sociodemographics, ideology, etc.).
External-Internal (E-I) Index (Krackhardt & Stern): \[
\text{E-I} = \frac{E_{\text{external}} - E_{\text{internal}}}{E_{\text{external}} + E_{\text{internal}}}
\]

Range: \([-1, +1]\)
\(-1\): Perfect homophily (all links within-group).
\(+1\): Perfect heterophily (all links cross-boundary).

title: Network science
text:
Macro-Level Structural Dimensions

Distance (\(d_{ij}\)): Length of the shortest path between \(i\) and \(j\).
Network Diameter (\(D\)): Maximum geodesic distance across any connected pair: \[
D = \max_{i, j \in V} d_{ij}
\]
Average Path Length (\(\langle d \rangle\)): \[
\langle d \rangle = \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} d_{ij}
\]
Effective Diameter (90th percentile): Minimum distance that connects 90% of reachable node pairs (robust to outliers).

Summary

What is a Graphical Model?

A framework to represent joint dependency structures and relationships between random variables.
Can be represented as:

Directed graphs (e.g., Bayesian networks, DAGs)
Undirected graphs (e.g., Markov Random Fields, partial correlation networks)

title: Network science
text:
In Pursuit of Causality

Finding causal relationships without expensive Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) is a primary research goal.
RCTs are often constrained by budgets, ethical barriers, and logistics.
The primary aim of these network graphs is to discover associations likely to indicate causal pathways.







Caveat Wasserman (2013)


RCT remains the gold standard. Any algorithmic causal discovery is an approximation reliant on structural and distributional assumptions.

title: Network science
text:
Marginal Correlation Networks

The most intuitive, but least informative network representation.
Directly transforms a correlation matrix into an undirected network:

An edge exists between \(i\) and \(j\) if \(\text{corr}(i,j) \neq 0\) (typically evaluated via hypothesis testing).
Can use Pearson’s \(r\), Kendall’s \(\tau\), or Spearman’s \(\rho\).









Merchant category correlation matrix and graph Leo et al. (2016)

title: Network science
text:
The Need for Partial Correlation

Marginal bivariate correlations can be spurious or explained away by third-party confounding variables.
Partial correlation \(p(X, Y \mid Z)\):

Correlation between residuals \(\epsilon_X\) and \(\epsilon_Y\) after linearly regressing \(X\) on \(Z\) and \(Y\) on \(Z\).

Connects directly to the precision matrix (inverse covariance matrix): \[\Omega = \Sigma^{-1}\]
The partial correlation matrix entries \(R(i, j)\) are: \[R(i, j) = -\frac{\Omega_{i,j}}{\sqrt{\Omega_{i,i}\Omega_{j,j}}}\]

title: Network science
text:
Conditional Independence: Gaussian Case
Let variables be jointly Gaussian: \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)\).






Theorem


Suppose \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)\). Then: \[X_i \perp \!\!\! \perp X_j \mid X_{-(i,j)} \iff \Omega_{ij} = 0\]




In Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs), testing for conditional independence is identical to testing if the off-diagonal elements of the precision matrix equal zero.

title: Network science
text:
Categorical / Multinomial Variables

For binary or categorical outcomes, Poisson / log-linear representations are used.
For two binary variables \(X = (x_1, x_2)\): \[\log p(x_1, x_2) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_{12} x_1 x_2\]
Parameter interpretations: \[\beta_{12} = \log \frac{p(0,0)p(1,1)}{p(1,0)p(0,1)}\]
Under independence, \(\frac{p(0,1)}{p(0,0)} = \frac{p(1,1)}{p(1,0)} \implies \beta_{12} = 0\).
Takeaway: Conditional independence corresponds to testing if the interaction/moderation parameter is zero.

title: Network science
text:
Common Targets of Inference
Researchers frequently need interval estimation and hypothesis testing rather than purely point estimates:

Edge existence: \(A_{ij} \neq 0\)
Edge difference: \(A_{ij} \neq A_{jk}\)
Centrality differences: Node strength, closeness, betweenness

title: Network science
text:
Analytical vs. Bootstrap Approaches

Analytical / Asymptotic Methods:

Established by Tony Cai and his colleagues (Cai and Ma (2013),Cai and Liu (2016),Cai (2017)) for Gaussian settings.
Limitations: Strictly requires Gaussianity; does not readily test centrality metrics.

The Bootstrap Solution:

Non-parametric or parametric resampling provides empirical distributions for:

Edge weights against zero (or arbitrary thresholds).
Confidence intervals around centrality measures and rank orderings Epskamp, Borsboom, and Fried (2018).

text:
Application: Comorbidity Networks







Network showing the relation between IGD, PHQ, and social withdrawal Fong et al. (2024)

title: Network science
text:
Challenges with High Dimensions
Computing empirical partial correlations directly encounters barriers:

Matrix Inversion: \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is unstable or non-invertible when \(p \ge n\).
Combinatorial Explosion: The number of conditional independence tests grows quadratically (\(\mathcal{O}(p^2)\)).

title: Network science
text:
Regularization: Graphical Lasso (glasso)

Penalizes the negative log-likelihood with an \(\ell_1\)-penalty to enforce sparsity: \[\hat{\Omega} = \arg\max_{\Omega \succ 0} \left( \ell(\Omega) - \lambda \sum_{j \neq k} |\Omega_{jk}| \right)\] where \[\ell(\Omega) = \frac{n}{2}\log|\Omega| - \frac{n}{2}\text{tr}(\Omega S_n) - \frac{nd}{2}\log(2\pi)\]
Tuning parameter (\(\lambda\)) selection:

Cross-Validation (CV)
Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC)

title: Network science
text:
Applications in Psychopathology

Psychological symptoms can be conceptualized as interacting elements in a complex network rather than passive indicators of an unobserved latent disease entity. :::{.columns}



Examples:

Depression & Suicidality: Junus and Yip (2024) demonstrated hopelessness scale items conditionally depend on suicide ideation.
Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD): Fong et al. (2024) identified gaming as a mood-escape mechanism directly connected to depressive mood and social withdrawal.










Hopelessness and Suicide Ideation Network Junus and Yip (2024)

title: Network science
text:
Network Estimation with bootnet
library(psychTools)
library(bootnet)
library(qgraph)

# Load sample data: Big Five Inventory (BFI)
data(bfi)
bfiSub <- bfi[, 1:25]

# 1. Marginal correlation network
Network_corr <- estimateNetwork(bfiSub, default = "cor")

# 2. Gaussian Graphical Model with EBICglasso
Network_BIC <- estimateNetwork(bfiSub, default = "EBICglasso")

# 3. Ising model for binary variables
Network_Ising <- estimateNetwork(bfiSub, default = "IsingFit")

# 4. Mixed Graphical Model (MGM) for mixed data types
Network_Mgm <- estimateNetwork(bfiSub, default = "MGM")

title: Network science
text:
Visualization & Centrality Testing
# Plot network layout using the Fruchterman-Reingold algorithm
plot(Network_BIC, layout = "spring")

# Compute and plot centrality indices (Strength, Betweenness, Closeness)
centralityPlot(Network_BIC)

# Test for statistical difference in edge strength
differenceTest(Network_BIC, "A1", "C2", "strength")

title: Network science
text:
Model Selection Guidelines







Summary of network model choices (adapted from network guidelines, 2024)

title: Network science
text:
Continuous Gaussian variables: Partial correlation via EBICglasso / GGM.
Binary variables: Ising models via IsingFit.
Mixed variables: Mixed Graphical Models (mgm).
Note: Continuous variables do not require an arbitrary shift between correlation and partial correlation; partial correlation graphs should generally be preferred to avoid spurious correlations.

title: Network science
text:
Motivation for ERGMs

Central Research Question: > Do individual attributes and local structural configurations drive the probability of tie formation?
Empirical research requires a statistical inference framework to:

Estimate effect sizes (\(\beta\) / \(\theta\))
Calculate standard errors and \(p\)-values
Control for endogenous network dependencies (e.g., reciprocity, transitivity)

title: Network science
text:
ERGM Problem Formulation
Let \(Y\) be an \(N \times N\) adjacency matrix of binary random variables \(Y_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\).
The general probability distribution of observing graph \(y\) is:
\[
P(Y = y \mid \theta) = \frac{\exp\left(\theta^\top g(y)\right)}{\kappa(\theta)}
\]

\(g(y)\): Vector of network statistics (counts of edges, mutual dyads, triangles, node-level covariates).
\(\theta\): Model parameters / coefficients to estimate.
\(\kappa(\theta) = \sum_{y^* \in \mathcal{Y}} \exp\left(\theta^\top g(y^*)\right)\): Intractable normalizing constant summing over all \(2^{\binom{N}{2}}\) possible networks.

title: Network science
text:
Local Conditional Interpretation: Change Statistics
Conditioning on the rest of the network (\(Y_{-ij}\)), the log-odds of a tie between \(i\) and \(j\) takes a logistic form:
\[
\text{logit}\left(P(Y_{ij} = 1 \mid Y_{-ij}, \theta)\right) = \theta^\top \delta(y)_{ij}
\]
where \(\delta(y)_{ij}\) is the change statistic:
\[
\delta(y)_{ij} = g\left(y_{ij}^{+}\right) - g\left(y_{ij}^{-}\right)
\]

\(y_{ij}^{+}\): The network with edge \((i, j)\) present.
\(y_{ij}^{-}\): The network with edge \((i, j)\) absent.

title: Network science
text:
Structural Elements of \(g(y)\)



Dyadic Independent Terms:

Density: Number of edges \(\sum y_{ij}\)
Nodal Covariates: Main effects of sender/receiver attributes (e.g., age, gender)
Dyadic Covariates: Homophily / absolute difference \(|X_i - X_j|\)

Dyadic Dependent Terms (Endogenous Structures):

Reciprocity: Mutual ties \(\sum y_{ij} y_{ji}\)
Triadic Closure: Triangles, transitive ties
Degree Distributions: Star terms, Geometrically Weighted Degree (GWESP, GWDegree)

title: Network science
text:
Dataset: Bott (1928) Children Imitation

Adopted from Robins et al. (2007)
Observational study of children’s playgroup behaviors (Bott, 1928).
A directed edge from \(i \to j\) indicates child \(i\) imitated child \(j\).
Analyzed in Bott’s 4th observation group (\(N = 11\), total possible directed dyads \(= 11 \times 10 = 110\)).

library(networkdata)
library(statnet)
data(bott)

# Inspect network and observed edge count
summary(bott[[4]] ~ edges)
## edges 
##    35

title: Network science
text:
Baseline Model: Bernoulli Random Graph
bottmodel.01 <- ergm(bott[[4]] ~ edges)
summary(bottmodel.01)
## ==========================
## Monte Carlo MLE Results:
##       Estimate Std. Error MCMC %  p-value    
## edges  -0.7621     0.2047      0 0.000313 ***
## ---
## Residual Deviance: 137.6 on 109 degrees of freedom
## AIC: 139.6   BIC: 142.3

Interpretation: \[\text{logit}(p) = -0.7621 \implies p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{0.7621}} \approx 0.318 = \frac{35}{110}\]
This recovers the observed density directly via maximum likelihood.

title: Network science
text:
Adding Nodal Attributes (In-Degree Covariate)
Hypothesis: Are older children imitated more frequently (higher in-degree)?
bottmodel_node <- ergm(bott[[4]] ~ edges + nodeicov('age.month'))
summary(bottmodel_node)
##                    Estimate Std. Error MCMC % p-value   
## edges              -2.89853    0.96939      0 0.00345 **
## nodeicov.age.month  0.05225    0.02272      0 0.02340 * 

Conditional Log-Odds: \[\text{logit}(P(Y_{ij}=1)) = -2.90 + 0.052 \times (\text{Age of child } j)\]
Effect:

For a 36-month-old target: \(-2.90 + 0.052(36) = -1.028 \implies P \approx 0.263\)
For a 48-month-old target: \(-2.90 + 0.052(48) = -0.404 \implies P \approx 0.400\)

title: Network science
text:
Adding Endogenous Structural Terms: Triangles
Triangles quantify transitivity and local clustering:
bottmodel_triangle <- ergm(bott[[4]] ~ edges + triangle)
summary(bottmodel_triangle)
##          Estimate Std. Error MCMC % p-value
## edges    -0.55772    0.58201      0   0.340
## triangle -0.05674    0.15330      0   0.712

Conditional Log-Odds: \[\text{logit}(P(Y_{ij} = 1 \mid Y_{-ij})) = -0.558 - 0.057 \times (\Delta \text{Triangles})\]

Tie creates 0 triangles: \(-0.558 - 0.057(0) = -0.558\)
Tie creates 1 triangle: \(-0.558 - 0.057(1) = -0.615\)
Tie creates 2 triangles: \(-0.558 - 0.057(2) = -0.672\)

title: Network science
text:
Why Standard Logistic Regression Fails

Standard GLMs assume independent observations (\(Y_{ij} \perp \!\!\! \perp Y_{kl}\)).
In networks with structural terms (e.g., triangle):

Whether tie \((i, j)\) forms a triangle depends on \((i, k)\) and \((k, j)\).
Dyadic dependence violates the \(i.i.d.\) assumption.

The normalizing constant \(\kappa(\theta) = \sum_{y^*} \exp(\theta^\top g(y^*))\) cannot be computed analytically (\(2^{\binom{N}{2}}\) states).
Solution: Markov Chain Monte Carlo Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MCMLE) via Metropolis–Hastings sampling.

title: Network science
text:
MCMLE Diagnostics
library(latticeExtra)
mcmc.diagnostics(bottmodel_triangle)

title: Network science
text:
Trace Plots: Should fluctuate stably around zero (white noise).
Density Plots: Should be centered at 0 and approximately bell-shaped.
Autocorrelation: Should decay rapidly toward zero as lag increases.
Geweke Diagnostic: Checks difference between early and late parts of the chain (\(p > 0.05\) indicates stationary convergence).

title: Network science
text:
Model Degeneracy






Caution on Naive Triangle Terms


Models with raw triangle counts frequently suffer from MCMC degeneracy: - The simulated chain collapses into either a completely empty graph or a complete clique. - Standard errors blow up, or MCMLE fails to converge.




Modern Solution: Use geometrically weighted terms with decreasing marginal returns:

gwesp (Geometrically Weighted Edgewise Shared Partner)
gwdgree / gwidegree / gwodegree

title: Network science
text:
Goodness of Fit (GOF)
We evaluate whether the fitted model reproduces higher-order network metrics not explicitly parameterized: Hunter, Goodreau, and Handcock (2008)
bottmodel_triangle_gof <- gof(bottmodel_triangle ~ model + odegree)
plot(bottmodel_triangle_gof)

title: Network science
text:
Solid line = Observed network value.
Boxplots = Values across networks simulated from fitted \(\hat{\theta}\).
If the observed line sits within the simulation intervals, the model fits well.

title: Network science
text:
Real-World Application









Network Study: Female sex worker network in Hainan Province Yu et al. (2016).
Structural Findings:

High transitivity and clustering within subgroups facilitated mutual safety and peer education.
However, customer contact networks showed structural holes due to economic competition.

title: Network science
text:
Summary

Random Graphs as Null Models:

ER graphs establish a baseline for completely random tie formation.
Small-world (WS) and Scale-free (BA) models highlight mechanisms producing high clustering and hubs.

ERGMs for Hypothesis Testing:

Model the full joint distribution of a network.
Change statistics evaluate individual attributes and local structural configurations simultaneously.

Robust Practice:

Always verify MCMC convergence (mcmc.diagnostics).
Guard against degeneracy using tapered terms (gwesp).
Confirm out-of-model fit via gof().
